summary: This single-center propensity score-matched cohort study evaluated HH-120, an IgM-like ACE2 fusion protein nasal spray, as treatment for SARS-CoV-2 infection in hospitalized patients in China. After PSM, 65 HH-120-treated patients showed significantly shorter median viral clearance time compared to 103 controls (8 vs 10 days, p<0.001), with an even larger effect in those with higher baseline viral load (7.5 vs 10.5 days, p<0.001). The safety profile was favorable with only mild adverse events; however, the non-randomized design limits causal inference.

No baseline demographic data available from abstract. Treatment-related AE denominator uses n=77 (pre-PSM enrolled), not n=65 (post-PSM analyzed).

summary: This 3-arm open-label RCT (n=72) tested twice-daily high-volume nasal irrigation with Johnson's Baby Shampoo/hypertonic saline (J&J/HTS) or hypertonic saline alone versus no intervention in adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 nasal infection, with the primary outcome of qRT-PCR nasal viral load over 21 days. Despite robust in vitro virucidal activity, J&J/HTS irrigation showed no reduction in viral load, viral shedding, or symptom scores compared to hypertonic saline alone or no-intervention controls at any timepoint; there was a marginally greater (worse) adjusted effect on viral load in the J&J/HTS arm versus control at day 1 (adjusted difference -5.277, 95% CI -9.474 to -1.080). Complementary in vitro pharmacokinetic studies demonstrated that the failure was attributable to rapid transepithelial absorption of the active long-chain detergent components of J&J Baby Shampoo from nasal surfaces, eliminating sustained virucidal contact.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All primary and secondary outcome numeric data (viral load Ct values over time, symptom scores, temperature) are presented only in figures (Figures 3A-D) — per-arm means/SDs/medians are not tabulated in the text, so arm_results values are null and result_source is 'not_reported'. The only quantitative between-group effect reported in text is the adjusted viral load difference for J&J/HTS vs. control at days 1 and 3. Viral shedding medians and IQRs are reported in the text. The effect size for viral shedding across all three groups is reported as epsilon-squared 0.004 (95% CI 0.0009-0.117) but no pairwise comparisons are given. The between_group_effect for arm1 vs arm3 at Day 1 is coded as a mean_difference but note the paper labels it 'adjusted effect difference' in Ct units (higher Ct = lower viral load; negative value means worse for J&J arm). Percent female was calculated from reported percent male (arm1: 38% male → 62% female; arm2: 50% male → 50% female; arm3: 58% male → 42% female). The 'effect size' column in Table 1 refers to epsilon-squared or Cramér's V for baseline balance, not treatment effects. No pairwise comparison between arm1 (J&J/HTS) and arm2 (HTS alone) is reported numerically in the text.

summary: This double-blind RCT (n=68) tested three doses of highly purified leucocyte interferon alpha (0.44, 1.52, or 4.4 Mu/day) versus placebo by intranasal spray twice daily for 28 days in healthy adult volunteers under natural exposure conditions. The high dose (4.4 Mu/day) produced no virologically confirmed colds and no post-treatment colds, but caused definite treatment reactions (protracted nasal discomfort, epistaxis) in 5/16 volunteers compared with 0/17 on placebo (p=0.02, Fisher's exact test); however, the overall rate of treatment discontinuation did not differ significantly across groups (log-rank p=0.49). The study concluded that the minimum effective interferon dose for prevention caused unacceptable local side-effects, preventing its use as long-term prophylaxis.

summary: This phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (CONTAIN study; n=450 healthy German adults, 99% vaccinated) tested 0.1% azelastine nasal spray 3 times daily for 56 days as pre-exposure prophylaxis against SARS-CoV-2. In the ITT analysis, PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection was significantly lower in the azelastine group (2.2%, 5/227) compared with placebo (6.7%, 15/223; OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.11–0.87; p=0.02), representing a ~67% relative reduction. Secondary endpoints corroborated the primary finding, including reduced symptomatic infection, longer time to infection among infected participants, shorter duration of RAT positivity, and fewer rhinovirus infections; adverse events were generally mild and comparable between arms.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Full text available. Per-protocol population was n=353 (azelastine n=179, placebo n=174). summary: This double-blind RCT tested intranasal recombinant interferon beta serine (12x10^6 U three times daily for ~4.3 days) against placebo in 40 healthy adults experimentally inoculated with rhinovirus type 39. Treatment did not significantly reduce clinical cold rates or symptom severity, but significantly reduced virus shedding on days 4 and 6 post-challenge (p=0.05 and p=0.06). In a substudy of 18 infected participants, interferon treatment was associated with significantly lower rates of bilateral eustachian tube dysfunction (23% vs 80% of subjects, p=0.05) and a non-significant reduction in middle-ear pressure abnormalities (18% vs 38% of observations), suggesting antiviral therapy may attenuate virus-associated middle-ear dysfunction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Eustachian tube function and MEP data are also presented in figures (Fig 1, Fig 2) with time-course data; daily proportions by timepoint are only available from figures and were not extracted per-day. The eustachian tube substudy randomized 20 subjects (14 interferon, 6 placebo), but 1 in each group did not become infected, leaving n=13 and n=5 for analyses. Total symptom score and nasal mucus weights are reported for ill subjects only (denominators not explicitly stated). Treatment duration: subjects received 2 doses on evening of day 1 post-challenge then 3x/day for 4 days = approximately 4.3 days total (stated as such in abstract). Follow-up was to day 21 post-challenge.

summary: HH-120, an IgM-like ACE2 fusion protein nasal spray, was evaluated as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) against SARS-CoV-2 Omicron (BA.5.2/BF.7) in three investigator-initiated trials in Beijing: NS01 (single-arm, n=12, with external control n=6, continuous close contacts); NS02-Part1 (RCT 2:1, n=186, general contacts); and NS02-Part2 (RCT 4-arm, n=64, close contacts). summary: This Phase II randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested Nasodine (0.5% povidone-iodine nasal spray, 8 doses/day for 3 days) versus a matched water placebo in 23 culture-positive adults with early SARS-CoV-2 (Omicron variant) infection in South Africa. summary: This paper reports a virological sub-study of a human challenge trial in which 28 volunteers received intranasal R61837 (a synthetic capsid-binding antiviral) and 18 received placebo after experimental inoculation with rhinovirus type 9 at the MRC Common Cold Unit. The primary finding is that drug-resistant RV9 emerged in the nasal passages of treated volunteers: 9 of 19 virus-positive treated volunteers shed resistant virus (versus 0/15 placebo), with resistance extending to cross-reactive agents (chalcone, DCF); clinical cold rates were 21% (6/28) in the treated arm versus approximately 50% (9/18) in placebo, but no statistical comparisons are provided. The paper demonstrates for the first time in humans that in vivo selection of drug-resistant rhinovirus occurs during antiviral nasal spray treatment, with important implications for clinical trial design.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily a virological/resistance sub-study, not a clinical efficacy report; clinical outcome data (cold incidence, symptom scores) are presented only briefly in Table 2 without statistical analysis. The cold incidence numbers (6/28 drug, 9/18 placebo) are stated in passing. Table 3 (daily virus isolation pattern) is heavily garbled due to OCR/encoding issues and could not be fully extracted. Individual MIC ratio data per volunteer are in Table 5 (verbatim per-volunteer values reported). Nasal wash drug concentration data (Table 4) are individual-level, not arm-level summaries; mean/SD not calculable from the text as presented. Treatment duration was 4 days in this first trial (drug stopped before volunteers left); a second trial with 6 days is referenced but not reported here. The n_randomized_total of 46 is calculated as 28+18. Cold incidence percentage for placebo arm (50%) is calculated as 9/18. Follow-up duration estimated as 9 days total (~1.3 weeks), treatment 4 days (~0.57 weeks), post-treatment follow-up 3 days (~0.43 weeks).

summary: This three-arm, triple-blinded RCT randomized 35 COVID-19-positive outpatients to 0.5% PVP-I, 2.0% PVP-I, or saline nasal sprays administered over 3 days and followed for 30 days. The primary outcome of nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 viral load (by RT-PCR Ct) declined similarly in all three arms over time, with no statistically significant difference in the rate of Ct change between either PVP-I concentration and saline (0.5% PVP-I: mean difference −0.35 cycles/hr, 95% CI −1.58 to 0.89; 2.0% PVP-I: −1.06, 95% CI −2.32 to 0.20). The 2.0% PVP-I group showed significantly higher rates of nasal burning (93% vs 17–29%) but significant within-group symptomatic improvement across all symptom domains; no worsening of olfaction occurred in any participant at 30 days.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Carrageenan increased recovery rate for coronavirus OC43/229E (RR=2.39), influenza A (RR=2.19), and rhinovirus (RR=1.70); CIs widely overlapping, consistent effects across virus types.
Carrageenan reduced recurrence for coronavirus (RR=0.40), influenza A (RR=0.35, ns), and rhinovirus (RR=0.43); all point estimates consistent with overall 56% reduction.
Carrageenan effect was heterogeneous by cold duration: minimal effect in quintiles 1-2 (0.24-0.25 days, 4-6%), moderate in quintile 3 (1.32 days, 15%), and largest in quintile 4 (3.85 days, 28%).

summary: This is an individual-patient data (IPD) re-analysis of two double-blind RCTs (Ludwig adult trial, N=203; Fazekas children trial, N=153) testing intranasal 0.12% iota-carrageenan (3x daily for 7 days) versus placebo for treatment of laboratory-confirmed common cold in Vienna, Austria. Among 254 virus-positive participants, nasal iota-carrageenan significantly increased the overall recovery rate (RR=1.54, 95% CI 1.15-2.1, p=0.003), with subgroup recovery RRs of 2.39 for coronavirus OC43/229E, 2.19 for influenza A, and 1.70 for rhinovirus. Carrageenan also reduced the risk of cold lasting >20 days by 71% (RR=0.29, p=0.003) and reduced symptom recurrence by 56% (RR=0.44, p=0.002); quantile analysis showed the greatest benefit for prolonged colds (28% shorter duration in quintile 4), with no meaningful effect on short colds.

summary: This cluster-randomized open-label controlled trial tested physiological seawater nasal irrigation (3 pumps × 3 times/day for up to 5 days) versus no treatment in 403 children aged 1-18 years with mild or asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.2 infection at a Fangcang shelter hospital in Shanghai. PSNI significantly shortened the duration of viral shedding (median 2.40 vs 3.09 days, p=0.014) and increased the proportion achieving viral negativity by day 5 (74.88% vs 56.78%, NNT=6), with the effect remaining significant after adjustment for age and vaccination status (HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.04-1.55, p=0.017). Benefits were more pronounced in unvaccinated children; no significant difference in adverse events was detected between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IQR values for DVS are reported as single numbers in Table 1 (2.14 for control, 1.13 for PSNI) — these appear to be the full IQR width rather than low/high bounds, so iqr_low/high left null. Symptom outcome data over days 1-5 appear primarily in figures (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 1) with only baseline counts extractable from Table 1; daily time-series data left as not_reported. The paper states 'mean reduction in viral shedding time was 0.37 days' which is extracted as the mean difference; this contrasts with the median difference of 0.69 days. Exact event counts for day-5 negativity were not explicitly stated — only percentages — so events not populated. Age IQR for PSNI group: median 5.11 (IQR 5.22); for control group: median 6.58 (IQR 6.89) — single IQR values only. Cluster randomization with only ~4 wards total (2 per group) is a major methodological limitation noted in RoB assessment.

summary: This double-blind placebo-controlled human challenge trial evaluated prophylactic intranasal CL 88,277 (1-phenyl-3-(4-phenyl-2-thiazolyl) guanidine), an experimental antiviral compound, against experimental rhinovirus 44 challenge in 20 seronegative healthy male volunteers. Rhinovirus illness developed in 5/10 subjects in each group (50%), with no statistically significant difference in illness incidence, severity, or symptom scores between arms. CL 88,277 appeared to reduce total virus isolates (25 vs. 37) and shortened the duration of virus shedding, with lower post-challenge serum antibody titers in the drug group (geometric mean titer 36.8 vs. 90.2 at day 28; p=0.055), suggesting partial inhibition of viral replication without clinically meaningful protection.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Daily sign and symptom scores (Table 2) are reported as group totals across all 10 subjects per arm, not as per-subject means or SDs, so mean/SD could not be extracted for that outcome. Serum antibody geometric mean titers are on a log scale (geometric means); these are reported as raw geometric means rather than logs. Day 0 and Day 8 serum antibody titer for placebo arm is listed as '<2' (below detection), which cannot be assigned a numeric value. The paper notes the challenge was conducted in January 1976. Adverse event counts for bad taste (90% = 9 subjects) were calculated from the stated percentage. No formal statistical testing was performed for illness incidence; p-values reported only for antibody titers (Student's t-test, one-tailed). Virus isolation data in Table 3 are counts of positive isolates per day per group, not per-subject rates (except for Day 2 where 9/10 placebo vs 6/10 drug-treated subjects excreted virus as stated in text). Time span of virus excretion difference was noted as 0.1>P>0.05 (Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney, one-tailed) — not statistically significant.

summary: This single-arm pharmacokinetic study challenged 28 healthy volunteers at the Common Cold Unit with human rhinovirus strains and measured the clearance of intranasally administered HuIFN-alpha2 (10^5 IU per nostril) before and after challenge. The primary finding was that the half-life of intranasal interferon (~20 minutes) was not significantly altered by rhinovirus infection or rhinorrhoea, suggesting that therapeutic concentrations could theoretically be maintained in the nose during a cold. This was not an efficacy trial — no comparator arm was used and the dose administered was explicitly stated to have no therapeutic effect on established experimental rhinovirus infection.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a pharmacokinetic study, NOT a comparative efficacy trial — it has no control arm and reports no between-group treatment effect. All quantitative outcome data (interferon concentrations at each timepoint) appear only in figures (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2) and cannot be extracted numerically. Correlation coefficients (r = 0.054, 0.058, 0.043 for 5-, 20-, 60-min samples) are reported verbatim in text. The 28 volunteers were all challenged with rhinovirus but interferon was administered only on assessment days (pre-challenge day and day 3 or 4 post-challenge) as a pharmacokinetic probe. This paper should likely be excluded from a meta-analysis of antiviral nasal spray efficacy trials as it contains no comparative efficacy data.

summary: This 7-arm open-label RCT (n=189) tested single-dose PVP-I nasal irrigation (0.4%, 0.5%, 0.6%) and nasal spray (0.5%, 0.6%) versus distilled water placebo in RT-PCR-confirmed symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 patients in Bangladesh, assessing nasopharyngeal viral clearance (RT-PCR negativity) 1-15 minutes post-intervention. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The outcome assessment was performed only 1-15 minutes after intervention — this is an extremely short virucidal activity window, not a clinical treatment follow-up. The control NI and control NS are separate placebo arms (arm 6 and arm 7 respectively); NI intervention arms are compared only to CNI, and NS intervention arms only to CNS. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled human challenge study tested intranasal interferon alpha-2a (Roferon-A) against RSV infection in healthy adult volunteers at the MRC Common Cold Unit. In the prophylactic trial (n=19 per arm), interferon alpha-2a significantly reduced the incidence of colds (1/19 vs 7/19, p<0.05) and mean total clinical score (3±6 vs 12±15, p<0.05) and nasal secretion weight (7±12 g vs 17±21 g, p<0.05) compared with placebo. In the therapeutic trial (n=10 interferon, n=11 placebo), there was no evidence that interferon alpha-2a reduced severity or duration of established RSV colds, with the only significant difference being a higher mean clinical score in the interferon group on day 2 (p<0.05), consistent with a local irritant effect.

summary: This 4-arm double-blind RCT tested three doses of intranasal recombinant consensus interferon alpha-1 (rIFN-αCon1: 3, 9, or 30 MU/day) versus placebo in 119 healthy adults over 25 days to assess nasal tolerance rather than antiviral efficacy. All three doses caused significantly higher withdrawal rates due to nasal adverse effects (55-67% vs 30% placebo, p<0.05) and significantly higher rates of moderate-to-marked lymphocytic infiltration on nasal biopsy (70-90% vs 10% placebo, p<0.05). The study concluded that rIFN-αCon1 does not have a more favorable therapeutic index for intranasal use than previously tested interferon-alpha subtypes, and that nasal inflammation risk correlates with interferon antiviral activity rather than protein content.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily a tolerance/safety study, not an efficacy trial; the primary endpoint was nasal tolerability. Rhinovirus illness data were incidental and the study was not powered for efficacy. Biopsy subset n values from abstract (N=10, N=9, N=13, N=10) differ slightly from methods section (10-12 per group); text summary values used as they give specific per-arm denominators. Exact withdrawal event counts back-calculated from percent figures stated (55%, 57%, 67%, 30%) cross-checked against Table 2. The percent for blood-in-mucus outcome provides proportions but not raw event counts — events left null. Between-group effect values not calculated per instructions for binary outcomes; p-values all reported as threshold p<0.05 only. Pairwise interferon-vs-interferon comparisons omitted as stated not significant. Cumulative withdrawal curve data is in Figure 1 (not extractable). Biopsy lymphocytic infiltration proportions are also displayed in Figure 2.

summary: This double-blind, 3-arm experimental rhinovirus challenge trial at the MRC Common Cold Unit tested prophylactic intranasal recombinant interferon alpha-2A alone, intranasal enviroxime alone, and their combination against rhinovirus types 9 and 14 in 51 healthy adult volunteers. The combination arm had the lowest rate of significant colds (23.5%) compared to IFN alone (35.3%) and enviroxime alone (47.0%), and the IFN-containing arms had approximately half the mean daily clinical scores of the enviroxime/placebo arm; however, none of the differences between any groups reached statistical significance. The study failed to demonstrate the anticipated marked synergy between IFN-alpha and enviroxime seen in vitro, likely because enviroxime is rapidly cleared from the nasal mucosa by the ciliary-mucous mechanism, preventing adequate contact with host cells.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Mean daily clinical scores and mean daily nasal secretion weights are presented only in figures (Figs. 1 and 2) with no tabular numeric values — these could not be extracted quantitatively. Proportion of volunteers excreting virus over time also presented only in figure (Fig. 3). The paper describes that IFN arms had 'half' the mean daily clinical scores of the enviroxime arm but gives no exact numeric values. Tolerance sub-study (n=11, no virus challenge) reported separately from the main challenge study. The 4 saline-challenge control volunteers (arm_id=4) served only as tolerability controls and are not formally part of the 3-arm efficacy analysis. Note: the note about serology states 17 sera in IFN/PEN group but only 15 in both other groups, which the authors flag as a potential bias source for virological outcomes. The arm_id=1 corresponds to IFN + enviroxime placebo (IFN/PEN); arm_id=2 to enviroxime + IFN placebo (enviroxime/PIFN); arm_id=3 to combination IFN + enviroxime; this assignment maximizes extraction of the primary intervention (IFN) as arm 1 per instructions, treating enviroxime monotherapy as the comparator.

summary: This Phase 1 paper reports two randomized, placebo-controlled, observer-blind dose-escalation studies (Study 101 in USA; Study 102 in EU) evaluating ALN-RSV01, an intranasal siRNA targeting RSV nucleocapsid protein, for safety and tolerability in 101 healthy adult male volunteers at single doses up to 150 mg or five consecutive once-daily doses. No serious adverse events occurred and the frequency, character, and severity of adverse events — predominantly mild nasopharyngeal examination findings such as nasal edema, mucosal erythema, and epistaxis — were similar between ALN-RSV01 and placebo (normal saline) across all dose levels. The study was not designed to test antiviral efficacy; no infection or virological outcome data were collected.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a Phase 1 safety/tolerability study with no antiviral efficacy endpoints — there are no infection incidence, viral load, or symptom score outcomes. All outcomes extracted are adverse event (safety) data from Tables 2, 3, and 4. Note that Study 101 active arm N=24 is the sum of five dose cohorts (5+4+5+5+5), and placebo N=10; Study 102 Part A active N=14, placebo N=11; Study 102 Part B active N=27, placebo N=15. Total ALN-RSV01 = 24+14+27 = 65, placebo = 10+11+15 = 36, total = 101. Between-group statistical test results (Fisher's exact, ANOVA) are described only qualitatively (no significant differences) without exact p-values in tables — no p-values extracted. Pharmacokinetic values in Table 5 are near-all below LLOQ with only a narrow range of detectable values (1.6–4.8 ng/mL range) for 150 mg cohort; not extracted as a formal outcome since no per-arm means/SDs are reported. Treatment duration for Part B (multiple dose) is 5 days = 0.71 weeks; single dose is <1 day; follow-up total is 30 days = ~4.3 weeks. Follow-up duration recorded as 4 weeks (30 days).

summary: This series of five placebo-controlled experimental rhinovirus challenge trials (MRC Common Cold Unit, UK, 1983) tested self-administered intranasal recombinant human interferon alpha-2 (HuIFN-alpha2) for prophylaxis against HRV9 and HRV14. Across the trials, doses of 2.28 MU given 4 times/day and 1 time/day (with challenge 2-3h after dosing) significantly reduced clinically diagnosed colds and antibody seroconversion (P<0.05–0.01), while 2.28 MU once daily with a 13-14h interval before challenge produced no detectable effect. The final trial at 3.85 MU three times/day (n=36; 17 interferon, 19 placebo) — challenging at the expected point of maximum susceptibility — demonstrated significant reductions in viral excretion, nasal secretion, and clinical scores despite a non-significant reduction in total colds (2/17 vs 5/19), supporting this regimen for large-scale field trials.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports five separate sub-trials within a single publication, each with different dosing regimens, making arm-level sample sizes complex: Trial 1 (2.28 MU x4/day): IFN n=11, placebo n=14 (virus-challenged); Trial 2 (2.28 MU x1/day, challenge 2-3h): IFN n=9, placebo n=11; Trial 3 (2.28 MU x1/day, challenge 13-14h): IFN n=8, placebo n=9; Trial 4 (dose-response, no placebo group — 0.0218 MU n=16, 0.223 MU n=24, 2.37 MU n=25 across two challenge timings); Trial 5/final trial (3.85 MU x3/day): IFN n=17, placebo n=19 of 36 analyzed (1 excluded for external rhinovirus, 2 for high pre-challenge titres). Clinical score and nasal secretion data are presented ONLY in figures (Figs 1-4) — exact values not extractable; p-values for these outcomes are from figures only. Dose-response Trial 4 geometric mean clinical scores extracted from Table 4: 0.0218 MU group: 6-7h=6.63, 10-11h=2.74 (pooled geometric mean ~4.37 calculated as approximate average for n=16 total); 0.223 MU: 6-7h=5.15, 10-11h=3.58 (pool ~4.37 for n=24); 2.37 MU: 6-7h=0.98, 10-11h=1.73 (pool ~1.36 for n=25) — these are geometric means per sub-group, not overall group means; mean calculations in outcome 4 are approximations. Table 4 column for antibody rises lists n=6,4,10 (0.0218MU), n=10,9,19 (0.223MU), n=4,8,12 (2.37MU) — these represent: antibody risers in 6-7h group, in 10-11h group, and total. Table 4 virus excretion column: 7,7,14 (0.0218MU); 9,11,20 (0.223MU); 3,6,9 (2.37MU). p-values stated only as thresholds (e.g. P<0.05, P<0.01), never exact. Adverse events reported from saline-challenged volunteers only (n=14 IFN, n=10 placebo) in Table 6 — data represent safety sub-group not virus-challenged group.

summary: The SHIELD Study is an ongoing crossover RCT (NCT04478019) evaluating twice-daily povidone-iodine nasal swabs plus four-times-daily chlorhexidine gluconate oral rinse for prevention of SARS-CoV-2 infection in 221 healthcare and essential workers over 10 weeks. This preliminary report presents only interim acceptability data: overall acceptability was 3.76/5 and 76% of respondents would use the intervention again, though 36% found it less acceptable than anticipated. Primary efficacy data (SARS-CoV-2 viral load from thrice-weekly nasal swabs) were not yet available at the time of reporting, and 9 of 20 adverse-event reporters withdrew due to side effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a conference abstract/preliminary report; primary efficacy outcome data (SARS-CoV-2 viral load reduction) are explicitly stated as pending ('laboratory analyses are ongoing'). No per-arm randomization numbers are given for the crossover design. The adverse event total of 20 and withdrawals of 9 are reported overall, not per-arm or per-phase. Acceptability n=74 and future-use n=56 appear to be different response denominators from the same survey cohort. The document also contains an unrelated adjacent abstract (COVID-19 vaccination and HCW transmission in South Korea, doi:10.1017/ash.2022.199) whose table data are not from the SHIELD study and were excluded. Source_is_abstract_only is set to false as methods and results text are present, but data completeness is very limited.

summary: This paper reports two double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized experimental rhinovirus challenge studies evaluating intranasal rhinovirus receptor murine monoclonal antibody (RRMA) nasal drops for prevention of HRV-39 infection in healthy seronegative adult volunteers. Study 1 (135 µg total RRMA, n=30) found no reduction in infection or illness rates. Study 2 (1 mg total RRMA, n=27) likewise found no significant reduction in overall infection or illness rates, but demonstrated a significant 1–2 day delay in the onset of viral shedding and cold symptoms, and significantly lower nasal mucus weights on day 3 and viral titers on day 2 post-challenge (p=0.01 for subjective cold on day 2), suggesting partial receptor-blocking activity at higher doses.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports TWO separate studies with the same two arms (RRMA vs placebo) but different doses and schedules; all outcomes are extracted per study. Viral titer data for Study 2 (Fig. 1) are reported only in figures with mean ± SEM — exact numeric values per arm not tabulated in the text, so result_source set to not_reported for outcome_id 22. summary: This double-blind RCT (n=160) evaluated 0.12% zinc sulfate nasal spray (4x daily, up to 14 days) versus placebo for treatment of naturally acquired upper respiratory illness in nonsmoking adults. Zinc spray had no effect on symptom duration (median 7 days in both groups, p=0.45), and after adjustment for baseline imbalance in symptom severity, there was only a transient and marginally significant reduction in total and nasal symptom scores on day 1 (p=0.02 each), with no significant differences on any other day. The authors concluded that 0.12% zinc sulfate nasal spray does not reduce the duration or clinically meaningful severity of the common cold.

The between_group_effects for Table 1 are reported as 'Zinc minus Placebo difference' with 95% CI — these are entered as mean_difference with arm1_vs_arm2 direction. summary: This double-blind RCT tested low-dose recombinant human interferon alpha-2b (rIFN alpha-2b) nasal spray (9x10^5 IU per administration, twice daily for 5 days) versus placebo in 1449 Chinese male military recruits during a 10-day observation period, with serological IgM seroconversion assessed at day 15 as the outcome. The intervention significantly reduced infection rates for influenza A (RR 0.23, p<0.001), influenza B (RR 0.23, p<0.001), parainfluenza viruses 1-3 (RR 0.23, p<0.001), and adenovirus species B (RR 0.41, p=0.043), but showed no statistically significant benefit against RSV (RR 0.28, p=0.177). Dry pharynx and mild epistaxis were significantly more frequent in the treatment arm, but no serious adverse events were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper note '§' for ± in the original. The analyzed N per virus varies substantially from the randomized N because subjects seropositive at baseline were excluded from each virus-specific analysis, and only a subset (n=548) were tested for ADV and RSV antibodies in addition to Flu-A/B/PIV1-3. Adverse event absolute counts were not provided for average rates in Table 6 (only percentages); only select daily counts for epistaxis on days 3-4 were given as absolute Ns. The 7 subjects who withdrew due to psychological fear of adverse events are not clearly allocated between arms. PP and ITT analyses are both captured as separate outcome objects (outcomes 1-5 PP; 6-10 ITT) to preserve all tabulated data. summary: This Phase III randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N=306 randomized; primary analysis in 133 high-risk mITT participants) tested nitric oxide nasal spray (NONS) self-administered six times daily for 7 days against placebo in Indian adults with mild SARS-CoV-2 infection (confirmed by RT-PCR) within 72 hours of symptom onset. NONS produced a statistically significantly greater mean reduction in nasal SARS-CoV-2 RNA through Day 8 compared to placebo (mean treatment difference -0.52 log10 copies/mL, 95% CI -0.92 to -0.12; p=0.010), with accelerated viral clearance at 24 and 48 hours (6.6-fold and 7.4-fold improvements respectively). A significantly greater proportion of NONS-treated patients achieved RT-PCR negativity by end of treatment (82.8% vs 66.7%; p=0.046), with a median time to viral clearance of 3 versus 7 days (HR 1.354; p=0.044), and the spray was well tolerated with no serious adverse events.

summary: This 4-arm double-blind RCT tested intranasal recombinant interferon alpha-2A (Roferal-A) at doses of 1.5, 3.0, and 6.0 MU/day versus placebo for 28-day seasonal prophylaxis of respiratory viral infections in 412 healthy Australian adults during a winter outbreak dominated by influenza A H3N2. summary: This double-blind RCT (N=40 healthy adults, Australia, 2021) evaluated the safety and tolerability of 1% astodrimer sodium nasal spray (a dendrimer-based barrier antiviral agent) applied four times daily for 14 days versus placebo, in healthy volunteers with no active respiratory infection. The primary endpoint was safety: TEAEs occurred in 63.3% of astodrimer participants vs. 80.0% of placebo participants, all of mild severity, with no SAEs, no withdrawals due to AEs, and no systemic absorption detected, supporting a benign safety profile. This was an exploratory safety trial with no efficacy endpoints (no infection or virological outcomes measured), so no conclusions regarding prevention or treatment of respiratory viral infections can be drawn.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a safety/tolerability trial only — no infection, virological, or clinical efficacy outcomes were measured. The placebo arm analyzed N=10 (one participant randomized to placebo in Cohort 2 was excluded before product administration due to haematuria on dipstick and replaced; the replacement participant is counted in the N=10). Total randomized is reported as 40 (safety population); the excluded/replaced participant brings total enrolled to 41. Cohort 1 subgroup (N=12 astodrimer, N=4 placebo) also had single-dose safety and PK assessed before proceeding to multiple dosing. Notable AEs per arm in Table 3 reflect 'potentially related' counts only; full TEAE counts by system organ class not tabulated in detail. No efficacy outcomes were extracted as none were measured. The throat irritation TEAE listed in Table 3 attributes 1 event to placebo (not astodrimer); the text body attributes it to astodrimer — Table 3 values used as primary source.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (CARVIN study; n=90) tested 0.1% and 0.02% azelastine hydrochloride nasal spray versus placebo administered three times daily for 11 days as treatment for outpatients with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 (predominantly alpha variant). The primary finding was that the 0.1% azelastine group had a significantly greater area under the curve of viral load decrease over 11 days compared to placebo (AUC 24.14 vs 18.89, p=0.007), and in the high-viral-load subgroup (Ct<25), Day 4 viral load reduction was significantly greater with 0.1% azelastine versus placebo (log10 1.90 vs 1.05, p=0.005). No serious adverse events were reported in any group, though the small sample size and industry funding limit interpretation.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT05358873) tested a nasal spray containing HPMC-formulated human IgG1 anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibodies (NAS) versus normal saline placebo in 36 healthy Thai adults (27 NAS, 9 placebo) administered thrice daily for 7 days. The primary finding was a significant and marked increase in nasal fluid SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibody levels (surrogate virus neutralization SIP%) after NAS application compared to baseline for ancestral, Delta, and Omicron BA.2 variants (median SIP immediately post-dose: 97.58%, 97.44%, and 94.65% respectively, all p=0.00012207 vs baseline), with effects persisting at 6 hours; no significant increase was seen in the placebo group. NAS was well tolerated with no treatment-emergent adverse events and no sinuscopic changes over 14 days, though the trial was not powered to detect clinical COVID-19 infection endpoints.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This is a safety/immunological mechanistic trial, not an efficacy trial for COVID-19 prevention — the primary outcome is nasal SIP (surrogate neutralization), not infection incidence. 2) Placebo arm SIP values at post-administration timepoints were not reported numerically in the text (stated as 'no significant difference' from baseline); exact placebo medians not extractable. 3) SIP data presented in figures (Fig 5b, 5c, 5d) as IQR boxplots — IQR bounds not reported in text, only medians and p-values. 4) P-values reported in scientific notation (1.2207E-4 and 6.1035E-05) converted to decimal equivalents. 5) Each participant was randomly assigned to only ONE post-dose collection timepoint (immediate OR 6h), not both — thus n per timepoint is a subset of 27 NAS participants but exact subgroup sizes are not stated. 6) SNOT-22 and TNSS outcomes reported as % of severity levels per symptom, not as total scores — only runny nose/rhinorrhea showed statistically significant between-group difference; all other SNOT-22 and TNSS items had adjusted p>0.9999. 7) The p-value for SNOT-22 runny nose is stated as <0.0001 (threshold, not exact); TNSS rhinorrhea p=0.0005 (exact). 8) Two participants excluded pre-randomization due to nasal polyps (screened n=38, randomized n=36). 9) Pseudovirus neutralization PVNT50 data (Table 1, preclinical) and biocompatibility data are preclinical/in vitro and not extracted as clinical outcome data.

summary: This single-blind RCT evaluated SA58, a broad-spectrum anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibody intranasal spray, as post-exposure prophylaxis in 1222 healthy adult workers at construction sites in Beijing within 72 hours of exposure to confirmed SARS-CoV-2 (Omicron BF.7) cases. In the modified efficacy analysis (n=1123), SA58 reduced laboratory-confirmed symptomatic COVID-19 by 80.82% (95% CI 52.41–92.27%) and SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR positivity by 61.83% (95% CI 37.50–76.69%) compared to placebo, both statistically significant. All adverse events were mild (Grade 1) with no serious adverse events or deaths, and adverse event rates were similar between arms (25% SA58 vs 22% placebo, p=0.49).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Full analysis set had 901 SA58 and 321 placebo participants; efficacy analysis excluded 99 participants (54 baseline RT-PCR positive + 45 positive within 24h of first dose), leaving n=824 SA58 and n=299 placebo. Median follow-up was very short (2.25 days SA58, 2.79 days placebo). The paper reports incidence rates per 100 person-days (not simple proportions) as the primary metric; crude IRRs are reported. Efficacy = 1 - IRR. Hazard ratios from Cox models are shown in Figure 2 but exact numeric values are not stated in the text (only in figures). Person-days at risk extracted from Table 2: SA58 symptomatic COVID-19 = 3162, SARS-CoV-2 PCR positive = 3078; placebo symptomatic COVID-19 = 1200, SARS-CoV-2 PCR positive = 1144. The trial ended prematurely due to Chinese COVID policy lifting on December 7, 2022, before target n=2300 was reached. No per-arm n_randomized is reported (only total randomized 1634 at 3:1 ratio, implying ~1226 SA58 and ~408 placebo randomized, but 401 not administered and 11 lost to follow-up). The full analysis set (n=901/321) represents those who were randomized and received at least one dose. Hazard ratios from Kaplan-Meier/Cox model appear in Figure 2 but exact values not extractable from text.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled experimental challenge study tested an intranasal low-pH citrate/phytic acid buffer spray (pH 3.5, 4x daily for 5 days) versus saline placebo in 44 healthy HRV16-seronegative adults inoculated with 1000 TCID50 HRV16. The study was underpowered for clinical endpoints and represents a proof-of-concept pilot demonstrating antiviral activity in vivo without demonstrable clinical benefit.

summary: This combined analysis of two parallel multicenter RCTs tested inhaled zanamivir (10 mg twice daily) with or without intranasal zanamivir (6.4 mg twice daily) versus placebo for 5 days in 417 adults with influenza-like illness, of whom 262 (63%) had confirmed influenza A or B. In confirmed cases, both zanamivir regimens reduced the median time to alleviation of major symptoms by 1 day versus placebo (4 vs 5 days; p=0.02 for inhaled+intranasal, p=0.05 for inhaled alone), with substantially larger benefits of 3 days in the pre-specified subgroups of febrile patients and those treated within 30 hours of symptom onset (p≤0.001). Intranasal zanamivir additionally reduced nasal viral titers compared with placebo, and both regimens were well tolerated with no significant increase in adverse events versus placebo.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Three-arm trial: arm_id=1 is inhaled+intranasal zanamivir (the more comprehensive intervention), arm_id=2 is inhaled zanamivir alone, arm_id=3 is placebo. Viral titre data (nasal washings) were collected only at 3 of 70 centers; exact per-arm means/SDs not reported in text — only mean differences vs placebo stated. Nasal washings substudy sample sizes not explicitly stated. HI antibody mean values are in log2 units. The p<0.001 for arm1 vs arm3 in the ≤30hr subgroup was reported as '<0.001' so p_value_exact set to false. summary: This double-blind RCT tested daily intranasal drops of human leukocyte-derived interferon-alpha (~5,000 IU/day) versus placebo over one winter season (December 1977–March 1978) in 86 Japanese adult volunteers (nursing students, elderly home residents, laboratory staff) for prevention of upper respiratory viral infections, primarily influenza and parainfluenza. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled experimental challenge trial tested prophylactic intranasal recombinant human interferon-beta serine (HuIFN-βser) in 54 evaluable healthy adult volunteers challenged with rhinovirus types 9 and 14 at the MRC Common Cold Unit. IFN-β significantly reduced virus shedding (14/27 vs 24/27, p<0.05 for proportion isolating virus at any time) and produced clinically meaningful reductions in significant colds (3/27 vs 9/27), mean clinical scores, nasal secretion weights, and days of virus excretion, though not all differences reached statistical significance individually. The treatment was well tolerated with minimal local adverse effects, supporting the prophylactic efficacy of intranasal IFN-β against experimental rhinovirus infection.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled experimental challenge trial at the MRC Common Cold Unit tested intranasal recombinant human interferon-gamma (rHuIFN-gamma, 1 MU per nostril 3x/day for 13 doses) against rhinovirus types 9 and 14 in 43 healthy volunteers. Unlike interferon-alpha and interferon-beta, rHuIFN-gamma failed to prevent clinical illness (53% vs 41%, NS) or virological infection (88% vs 82%, NS); paradoxically, treated volunteers had significantly higher mean total clinical scores (22.8 vs 13.4, p=0.024), suggesting rHuIFN-gamma may enhance rather than inhibit rhinovirus disease. The agent also caused blood-stained nasal secretions and frank nosebleeds exclusively in the active treatment group.

summary: This double-blind placebo-controlled human experimental challenge study tested intranasal lymphoblastoid interferon (Wellferon, 13.5 MU/ml) given three times daily for ~4 days for prevention of rhinovirus (HRV9+HRV14) and influenza A (H3N2) infections in healthy volunteers at the MRC Common Cold Unit. In the rhinovirus trial (n=42 analysed), IFN completely prevented significant colds (0/19 vs 7/23, p<0.05), significantly reduced total clinical scores (p=0.043) and nasal secretion weights (p=0.016), and reduced the combined endpoint of virus shedding or antibody rise (74% vs 100%, p<0.05). In the influenza A trial (n=30 analysed), IFN approximately halved illness frequency (31% vs 59%) but the difference was not statistically significant, and no reduction in virological infection rates was observed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports TWO separate experimental challenge trials (rhinovirus and influenza A) in a single publication, both with the same 2-arm design; outcomes are reported separately by trial. Arm-level sample sizes for the saline-challenged control group (22 volunteers total, 6 IFN + 10+ placebo) are not included in primary efficacy analyses. Continuous outcome data (mean daily clinical scores, nasal secretion weights, daily virus shedding proportions) are presented only in figures (Figs 1 and 2) without tabulated numeric values — result_source set to 'not_reported' for these arms. For Trial 1, the IFN group antibody titer stratum sizes are not individually stated in the text (only totals). For Trial 2, the individual stratum N values for the IFN group are not stated. The p-values for clinical scores and nasal secretion in Trial 1 (p=0.043 and p=0.016) are verbatim from text. The influenza trial clinical score difference described as 'significant on two days' and 'close to 0.05 for one other comparison' — no exact p-values given. Antibody rise event count for Trial 2 IFN arm (n=9) is calculated from Table 2 subgroup sums (4+5+0=9). The paper reports '31%' for influenza IFN illness and '59%' for placebo — verbatim percentages used; 4/13=30.8% and 10/17=58.8% confirm these. n_randomized_total of 96 is calculated from 57 (rhinovirus trial) + 39 (influenza trial).

summary: This double-masked RCT tested intranasal interferon alpha-2b combined with oral chlorpheniramine and ibuprofen (full treatment) versus anti-inflammatory drugs alone or double placebo as treatment for experimental rhinovirus type 39 colds in 150 healthy adults, with treatment initiated 24 hours after viral challenge. The full combination significantly reduced total symptom scores (by 33-73% in symptomatic subjects), rhinorrhea, sneezing, nasal obstruction, sore throat, cough, nasal mucus production, tissue use, and virus concentrations compared with placebo, with most reductions reaching statistical significance; the IFN component added measurable benefit beyond the anti-inflammatory drugs alone. Side effects were mild and similar across groups, though drowsiness was significantly more common in both active oral medication arms (p=0.03).

The 139 antibody-free subjects in Table 1 are a subset of the 150 ITT population; the illness rate denominator uses infected subjects (51, 52, 27), not the full ITT. summary: This multicenter, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial tested daily intranasal interferon alpha (IFNα) spray at 40,000 IU for 90 days versus saline placebo as primary prophylaxis against COVID-19 and other respiratory viral infections in 433 adult cancer patients in Australia. In the ITT population, IFNα significantly reduced COVID-19 incidence by 40% (8.3% vs 14.4%; RR 0.60, 95% CrI 0.33–0.97), with a stronger effect in the per-protocol cohort (RR 0.50, 95% CrI 0.26–0.84). There was no significant effect on other respiratory viral infections, severity, hospitalization, or mortality, and the spray was well tolerated with no significant safety concerns.

summary: BRL 5907, a double-stranded RNA polynucleotide interferon inducer of fungal origin given intranasally at 5 mg/day for 3 days, was tested against experimental challenge with rhinovirus type 4 in 12 seronegative volunteers (6 treated, 6 placebo) in a double-blind controlled trial at the Common Cold Unit, Salisbury, UK. summary: This paper reviews six controlled human challenge trials testing topical nasal application of CP 20961 (N,N-dioctadecyl-N',N'-bis(2-hydroxyethyl) propanediamine), a synthetic interferon inducer, against rhinovirus types 21, 25, and 41 in antibody-free healthy volunteers, for both prevention and treatment. Multiple-dose regimens (12 doses pre-challenge, 5 split doses, or 15 post-challenge doses) all reduced illness incidence and symptom severity compared to controls, with the 5-dose split regimen showing statistically significant reductions in viral shedding (P<0.05), illness rate (P<0.05), and symptom severity (P<0.01). Paradoxically, a single pre-challenge dose of drug significantly worsened outcomes (22% increase in virus-positive specimens, P<0.001), highlighting that efficacy was highly dependent on dosing regimen and timing relative to viral challenge.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a review/summary of six separate trials rather than a single trial; per-arm n are not given for each regimen — only total subjects per study group are provided in Table 1 (14, 50, 35, 15 across 6 studies). Interferon titer and viral shedding data for individual experiments appear primarily in figures (Figures 1-4) rather than tables; exact values extracted from figures should be treated as approximations. The n=50 for the 3+2 regimen spans three separate studies. Arm-level per-arm n breakdown between drug and vehicle is not reported. The 'between_group_effects' effect_value fields for rate of infection, illness, and symptom severity are encoded as proportion differences (e.g., -0.17 = 17% reduction) since the paper reports only '% difference from simultaneous controls' without providing denominators. Saline arm (arm_id=3) was used only in the single-dose experiment (n=35 total across drug/vehicle/saline). Oral lactose (arm_id=4) used only in therapeutic trial (n=15 total). summary: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled experimental challenge trials evaluated therapeutic intranasal recombinant interferon alpha-2 (HuIFN-a2, 2.7×10^7 IU/day for 5 days) initiated 28 hours after rhinovirus type 39 inoculation, delivered by nasal spray (n=23) or drops (n=29) in healthy adult volunteers. summary: Two placebo-controlled, double-blind experimental rhinovirus challenge trials tested intranasal IFN-a2 (recombinant) for prevention of RV type 39 infection in susceptible healthy adult volunteers: Study 1 used a multiple-dose regimen (11.4×10^6 IU four times daily for 4 days; n=12/arm) and Study 2 a once-daily regimen (42.8×10^6 IU/day for 5 days; n=14/arm). summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled rhinovirus challenge trial tested two doses of intranasal recombinant leukocyte A interferon (rIFN-aA) — 2.4 × 10^6 units/day and 0.7 × 10^6 units/day for 4 days — against experimental rhinovirus type 13 (RV13) challenge in 56 analyzable normal healthy adult volunteers. The 2.4M dose significantly reduced illness frequency (29% vs. 73% in placebo, p=0.032) with 60% efficacy, while the 0.7M dose had no significant effect on illness (67% vs. 63%); neither dose reduced infection rates. A separate 26-day tolerance study showed that 15% of 2.4M recipients developed nasal mucosal erosions and bloody mucus (vs. 0% placebo), whereas only 5.5% of 0.7M recipients had treatment-related adverse effects, demonstrating a dose-dependent trade-off between efficacy and local tolerability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports two separate sub-studies: (1) a challenge study in 56 analyzable volunteers and (2) a 26-day tolerance study in 57 analyzable volunteers; arms, doses, and sample sizes differ between the two sub-studies. In the challenge study, two separate placebo groups were used (n=16 for the 0.7M comparison, n=15 for the 2.4M comparison); some placebo volunteers contributed to both groups — this shared placebo design inflates effective N. summary: This double-blind RCT tested intranasal IFN-alpha-2 (2 x 10^6 IU/day for 28 days) versus placebo in 413 Australian hospital and research staff during the 1983 autumn, for prevention of natural respiratory viral infection. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports TWO separate studies: (1) a 25-day tolerance study (n=120, no viral challenge, no infection outcomes) and (2) an efficacy/challenge study (n=34). Both are 3-arm RCTs with identical dose assignments. Sample sizes in sample_sizes and baseline_demographics refer to the TOLERANCE study (n=40 per arm) as it is the larger study; the efficacy study per-arm Ns are 12/11/11. The total n_randomized_total (154) is the sum across both studies. The tolerance study has no infection or illness outcomes; all infection/illness outcomes are from the efficacy study. Daily symptom data for the tolerance study (Table 1, 15 symptoms × 3 arms × 3 columns) is not extracted as individual outcomes to manage size — full table data is available in the paper. Efficacy study seronegative subgroup results (n=10/9/10) largely mirror the full-cohort results and are extracted as secondary outcomes (outcome_id 15–17). summary: This double-blind RCT (n=550) evaluated intranasal recombinant interferon alpha-2b (IFN-a2b) for seasonal prophylaxis against natural rhinovirus and parainfluenza infection in University of Michigan students. In the primary twice-daily cohort (n=400; 1.5x10^6 IU/nostril BID x 4 weeks), IFN-a2b reduced rhinovirus infection by 76% (6/198 vs 25/198, p<0.01) but did not prevent parainfluenza infection; it did significantly reduce symptom severity in all cultured illness episodes (max severity 4.3 vs 6.4, p<0.05). However, substantial nasal side effects occurred including blood-tinged mucus (49% vs 16%), bleeding points, and mucosal ulcers/erosions in ~20% of treated participants by week 4, leading the authors to conclude that prolonged twice-daily use is inappropriate for healthy adults; a once-daily pilot (n=150) showed a trend toward maintained efficacy (59% reduction in rhinovirus infection) with fewer side effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Two parallel RCTs reported in one paper: primary twice-daily trial (n=400, arms 1-2) and pilot once-daily trial (n=150, arms 3-4). Note that n=198 per arm in twice-daily trial reflects analyzed participants after 6 withdrawals from arm 1 and ~1 from arm 2 (total n=400 randomized, n=396 analyzed per Table 1 note). Pilot study arm sizes: IFN arm n=75, placebo arm n=74 after 1 withdrawal. Blood-tinged mucus n calculated as 49% of 198=97 for arm 1, 16% of 198=32 for arm 2. Dry nose n calculated as 35% of 198=69 for arm 1, 27% of 198=53 for arm 2. The n=198 for primary trial arms is stated in Table 1 and Table 2 notes. P-values for symptom severity outcomes (max severity and max symptoms, all episodes) are stated as p<0.05 and p<0.001 for parainfluenza episodes. For rhinovirus-only episodes no significant p-values were reported. The number of episode observations used in Table 3 (79 IFN, 80 placebo for all episodes; 8 vs 28 rhinovirus; 14 vs 11 parainfluenza) reflect illness episodes from which cultures were collected, not all participants. No CIs are reported for any outcome. Protective efficacy of 76% stated verbatim but no RR or CI provided; RR calculated from raw counts. Pilot once-daily efficacy 58.6% stated verbatim. Antibody rise data for parainfluenza (5 IFN vs 3 placebo additional infections) not entered as separate outcome due to incompleteness. Total symptom score during episode also noted as significant but no values provided.

summary: This exploratory open-label single-arm trial evaluated SA58 nasal spray — a broad-spectrum anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibody administered intranasally — for prevention of household transmission of SARS-CoV-2 (Omicron BF.7) in 70 family contacts in Beijing, China, compared against a contemporaneous non-randomized external control group (n=362). summary: This non-randomized within-subject study in healthy adult volunteers (Baylor College of Medicine, 1978) tested intranasally applied human leukocyte interferon at doses of 8,000–80,000 U, delivered either by nasal drops or saturated cotton pledget, for prophylaxis against respiratory viral infection, using ex vivo VSV challenge of scraped nasal epithelial cells as the outcome. The study demonstrates proof-of-concept for topical interferon-induced antiviral activity in nasal epithelium but does not report clinical infection outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study is an ex vivo/mechanistic experiment — the 'outcome' is VSV yield from scraped nasal cells challenged in vitro, not in vivo respiratory infection incidence. Arm sample sizes are given only as number of cell-sample tubes (parenthetical values in tables), not as number of distinct volunteers per condition; each experiment pooled cells from 'at least three volunteers'. The paper does not report total volunteer N, randomization, or blinding. Table 2 uses the notation 'n_analyzed' to refer to tubes of 3×10^5 cells, not individual volunteers. The p-value threshold reported is p<0.025 (Student's t test); no exact p-values given. All significant results are reported as p<0.025. The 50,000 U drops condition (arm_id=3) had only 2-3 sample tubes. This study is primarily a dose-finding and delivery-method comparison, not a clinical efficacy trial. Effect sizes expressed as log10 VSV yield reduction. Arm ids 4 and 5 were both labelled 'cotton pledget' with different dose levels; multiple experiments reused arm_id=4 label for different doses — outcome objects specify doses in their names for disambiguation. No formal between-group statistical comparisons were reported for non-significant conditions; significance was reported only for conditions meeting p<0.025 threshold.

summary: This two-site, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled human challenge study tested CP-28,888-27 (N,N-dihexadecyl-m-xylylenediamine), a low-molecular-weight intranasal interferon inducer, against experimental rhinovirus type 13 and type 21 infection in 62 healthy adult male volunteers for prevention of infection and illness. summary: This double-blind RCT tested intranasal recombinant alfa-2b interferon at 10 or 20 MU/day (nasal spray, 4x daily for 5 days) versus placebo for treatment of naturally occurring common colds (predominantly rhinovirus) in 220 evaluable adults presenting within 48 hours of symptom onset. Although interferon significantly reduced rhinovirus shedding at days 5 and 7 compared to placebo (15-16% vs 47-48% positive, p<0.02), this antiviral effect did not translate to clinical benefit and was accompanied by significantly higher rates of nasal bleeding and bacterial complications requiring antibiotics.

summary: This cluster-randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested intranasal recombinant IFN-α2b (5×10^6 IU on day 1, 2.5×10^6 IU/day on days 2–5) as postexposure prophylaxis against rhinovirus illness in 199 community families in Tecumseh, Michigan during autumn 1985. Among 434 individual prophylaxis courses per group, IFN failed to reduce symptomatic cold episodes at any timepoint — in fact, cold episode rates were numerically higher in IFN recipients than placebo for all cycles and all virus subgroups (e.g., 7.6% vs 4.8% during therapy for all cycles), though none of the differences were statistically significant. However, IFN did significantly reduce rhinovirus isolation rates during and immediately after therapy (12.5% vs 58.8%, P<0.005 at 5 days), indicating the reduced dose was virologically active but insufficient to prevent symptomatic illness, concluding that postexposure prophylaxis requires at least 5×10^6 IU/day throughout the full course.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Unit of analysis throughout is individual prophylaxis courses (n=434 per arm), not individual participants; families with no spray use (13 IFN families, 10 placebo families) were excluded from analysis. The paper reports P>0.05 (not significant) for the 14-day rhinovirus isolation comparison. Follow-up total duration estimated from trial period late August to mid-November 1985 (~11 weeks). summary: This paper reports the development and psychometric validation of the SPRAY PAL questionnaire — a product acceptability instrument — within the context of the PREVENT-CoV phase 1 clinical trial of Q-Griffithsin (Q-GRFT) intranasal spray for COVID-19 prophylaxis. The paper does not report any clinical efficacy outcomes (infection rates, viral load, symptom scores) or quantitative safety outcomes; it reports only Cronbach's alpha, intraclass correlation coefficients, and convergent/discriminant validity statistics for the questionnaire. The SPRAY PAL was found to have adequate internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and validity across its acceptability, feasibility, and tolerability subscales in a combined sample of 40 healthy volunteers.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT eligible for inclusion in a meta-analysis of antiviral nasal spray clinical outcomes. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT evaluated intranasal pirodavir (R77,975) spray for treatment of naturally occurring rhinovirus colds in 201 adults, with primary analysis restricted to the 108 rhinovirus-confirmed participants. Despite significantly reducing rhinovirus shedding on days 3 (23% vs 70%, p<0.001) and 5 (12% vs 38%, p=0.002), pirodavir provided no clinical benefit: illness duration was identical (median 7 days in each group) and no differences in individual symptom scores were detected. summary: This paper reports four double-blind, placebo-controlled experimental rhinovirus challenge trials of intranasal pirodavir (R77975), a broad-spectrum capsid-binding antiviral agent, administered as 2 mg metered pump spray. In the single prophylaxis trial using six-times-daily dosing (25 total doses), pirodavir significantly reduced infection rate (58% vs 100%, p=0.015), clinical colds (8% vs 54%, efficacy 85%, p=0.03), virus shedding, and abnormal middle-ear pressures; three-times-daily dosing in two further prophylaxis trials showed no significant benefit. Initiated 24 hours after rhinovirus challenge, six-times-daily treatment significantly reduced virus shedding days but produced no clinical symptom benefit, and intranasal pirodavir was generally well-tolerated with excess transient unpleasant taste as the main adverse effect.

summary: This report describes three double-blind, placebo-controlled experimental rhinovirus (HRV) challenge trials in 202 healthy volunteers testing intranasal ruprintrivir (a HRV 3C protease inhibitor, 8 mg/dose, 2% suspension spray) for prophylaxis (2×/day or 5×/day for 5 days, starting 6 h before inoculation) and treatment (5×/day for 4 days, starting 24 h post-inoculation). Prophylaxis with ruprintrivir significantly reduced positive viral culture rates versus placebo (5×/day: 44% vs 70%, p=0.03; 2×/day: 60% vs 92%, p=0.004) and viral AUC, but did not reduce clinical cold frequency. Early treatment significantly reduced mean total daily symptom scores by 33% (2.2 vs 3.3, p=0.01), and also reduced respiratory symptom scores, nasal discharge weights, and viral titers, though cold incidence was not significantly reduced; ruprintrivir was well tolerated with primarily mild local nasal adverse effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper reports three separate trials (5x/day prophylaxis, 2x/day prophylaxis, 5x/day treatment) analyzed jointly. Arms 1-4 are prophylaxis arms from two separate trials; arms 5-6 are from the treatment trial. The treatment study primary p-value is stated as both p=0.014 in abstract and p=0.01 in Table 3 — Table 3 value used as it is the efficacy-evaluable analysis. Day-by-day viral titer, viral RNA, symptom score, and individual symptom score data appear only in figures (Figs 1-5) and are not extractable as numeric tables; these time-course data are noted as 'data only in figures'. The n for 'colds' denominators in prophylaxis arms are the 'infected' subsets (arm1: n=14, arm2: n=21, arm3: n=20, arm4: n=23 inferred from Table 2 infected counts). All p-values in this study are one-sided per protocol. The treatment study ANCOVA was adjusted for treatment, study site, challenge virus strain, and baseline values. The 2x/day prophylaxis ruprintrivir arm had n=26 randomized but n=25 evaluable (1 excluded).

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT conducted in Japan during the 1995 influenza season tested inhaled zanamivir (10 mg twice daily) with or without intranasal zanamivir (6.4 mg twice daily) against double placebo for 5 days in 116 adults with acute influenza-like illness. Combined zanamivir treatment significantly reduced time to alleviation of the three major influenza symptoms (fever, headache, myalgia) compared with placebo (median 3 vs. 4 days; P=0.0017), as well as time to alleviation of five symptoms, fever resolution, resumption of daily activities, and sleep disturbance improvement. Addition of intranasal zanamivir to inhaled zanamivir provided no additional benefit over inhaled zanamivir alone, suggesting lower respiratory tract replication is the primary driver of symptom pathogenesis.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled human challenge study tested once-daily intranasal zanamivir spray (6.4 mg) in three dosing regimens — a single dose 48 hours before inoculation, a single dose 4 hours before inoculation, or daily for 3 days starting 4 hours before inoculation — against experimental influenza A/Texas/91 (H1N1) infection in 47 sero-susceptible healthy volunteers. Both regimens that included zanamivir 4 hours prior to inoculation significantly reduced viral shedding (8% and 10% vs 78% placebo), with protective efficacies of 89% and 87% respectively; the 3-day regimen also significantly reduced infection (10% vs 78%, P<0.05), while the 48-hour pre-inoculation single dose did not confer significant protection. Significant reductions in nasal mucus weight were observed in the two groups receiving zanamivir 4 hours before challenge, though differences in symptom scores and URI rates were not statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper reports two separate studies: a pharmacokinetics study (n=36, three groups: nasal spray, nasal drops, inhaled) and an efficacy challenge study (n=47, four arms). Only the efficacy study is extracted as outcomes here as the pharmacokinetics study has no control arm and is not a comparative efficacy study. The paper does not report exact p-values for statistical comparisons of viral shedding for arm1 vs arm4. URI event counts per arm are not provided numerically (only described as non-significant); percent female for arm3 is calculated as 5 females out of 11 randomized (note: table shows 5/6 sex ratio which sums to 11 not matching n=11 total — one subject's sex may be missing or table reflects F/M among 11). The placebo arm n in Table 4 is 9 (3 excluded post-randomization). Between-group effect values for nasal mucus weight are not calculable from medians; p-values extracted from text. Protective efficacy percentages and 95% CIs reported in text: arm2 vs arm4 viral shedding PE=89% (95% CI 28-98%), infection PE=57% (95% CI -3 to 82%); arm3 vs arm4 viral shedding and infection PE=87% (95% CI 15-98%) — these are PE not standard effect measures and not directly entered in between_group_effects fields. AEs reported pooled across active arms for the efficacy study, not per arm.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled human influenza A (H3N2) challenge study tested intranasal INNA-051 (a TLR2/6 agonist nasal spray) at 150 µg and 300 µg given prophylactically (two doses on Days -4 and -1) versus placebo in 119 healthy adults. The pre-specified ITT primary analysis found no significant treatment effect on laboratory-confirmed infection incidence (45% placebo, 53% INNA-051 150µg, 59% INNA-051 300µg), partly due to unexpectedly low infection rates and undetected pre-existing immunity. In a post hoc analysis restricted to seronegative, PCR-confirmed infected participants (mITT-i), INNA-051 300µg significantly shortened the duration of quantifiable viral shedding by approximately 26 hours compared to placebo (p=0.0173) and reduced viral load on Day 7 (p=0.0465), with acceptable tolerability and no serious adverse events.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This paper reports TWO separate studies: a First-in-Human (FIH) dose-escalation safety/PK/PD study (SAD/MAD, n=64, Australia) and a human influenza challenge study (n=119-123, UK). The structured extraction above covers only the challenge study (the controlled efficacy trial with a placebo arm). The FIH study has no placebo-controlled efficacy outcomes extractable for meta-analysis. 2) Most quantitative viral load (VL-AUC, peak VL, VL-AUC over time) and symptom score data for the challenge study appear only in figures (Figures 5b-d, supplementary figure S5) — exact per-arm means, SDs, and AUC values are not reported in the text. 3) The paper reports combined 80.5% TEAE rate for both INNA-051 arms without separating 150µg and 300µg arm-specific counts; per-arm n_any_ae not calculable. 4) The mITT-i subgroup is explicitly a post hoc analysis, not the pre-specified primary analysis. 5) Baseline demographics (age mean/SD, sex) are stated to be in supplementary tables S1/S2 which are not provided in the text. 6) The 300µg arm had 9/41 (22%) participants excluded from mITT-i due to HAI >10 at admission; for 150µg it was 14/38 (37%); for placebo 8/40 (20%), creating differential post-randomization exclusion that may bias the mITT-i results. 7) Omitted primary endpoints for which no numeric data are in the text: VL-AUC, peak viral load, TSS-AUC, peak symptom score — all reported as non-significant in ITT but exact values are in figures only.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: In ITT, carrageenan significantly reduced disease duration in all three virus subgroups: hRV by 1.9 days (p<0.05), hCV by ~3.9 days (p<0.01), InfA by 3.3 days (p<0.05). In PP, significant reduction for hRV (1.8 days, p<0.05) and hCV (3.1 days, p<0.01), but not InfA (1.7 days, NS).

In ITT, carrageenan significantly reduced relapses per patient in hRV (0.13 vs 0.79, p=0.04), hCV (0.20 vs 0.58, p=0.007), and InfA (0.13 vs 0.79, p=0.04). In PP, only hCV subgroup reached significance (0.18 vs 0.53, p=0.006).

summary: This pooled individual patient data analysis of two double-blind RCTs (n=254 virus-confirmed common cold patients, children and adults in Austria) tested iota-carrageenan nasal spray (0.12%, 3x/day for 7 days) versus saline placebo for treatment of acute common cold. Carrageenan significantly reduced disease duration by approximately 1.9 days (ITT, p=0.002) and 1.7 days (PP, p=0.016), reduced relapses (average 0.17 vs 0.45 per patient, ITT, p=0.002), and produced significantly greater viral titer reductions at days 3–5 (median −2.2 vs −1.1 log[x+1], ITT, p=0.022). Subgroup analyses showed significant benefit across rhinovirus, coronavirus, and influenza A infections, with the largest effect in coronavirus-infected patients (~3.9-day reduction, p<0.01).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is an individual patient data (IPD) pooled analysis of two previously published RCTs (Fazekas 2012, n=213; Ludwig 2013, n=211), not a primary trial. Only virus-positive patients (n=254 ITT) are included in this analysis. Per-arm means and SDs for the primary outcome (duration of disease) are not provided as absolute values in the overall population — only differences are stated. Values presented in Table 6 for subgroup durations use ± which the paper indicates is SE not SD. Per-arm sample sizes within virus-specific subgroups are not provided numerically (only percentages of arm totals in Table 5). Improvement/deterioration percentages by arm for viral status change (Figure 4) are only in figures and could not be extracted. Serious AE count across both studies combined was 6 patients, but per-arm distribution is not stated. The SE values in the PP population virus clearance results (0.14 ± 0.7 and 0.38 ± 0.7) appear to be a likely typographical error in the paper (SE should be much smaller than 0.7); extracted verbatim. Relapses frequency data in Figures 3 and 6 are primarily in figures — only numeric averages per patient were extracted from text.

summary: This proof-of-concept double-blind RCT (n=45) tested intranasal chlorpheniramine maleate (CPM) 0.4% spray three times daily for 7 days versus saline placebo in unvaccinated Venezuelan outpatients with mild PCR-confirmed COVID-19. summary: This double-blind RCT (ICICC trial) tested iota-carrageenan nasal spray (0.12% in 0.5% saline, 4x/day for up to 10 days) versus saline placebo in 200 adults with early common cold symptoms at a single UK university site. The primary endpoint (mean total symptom score Days 2-4) was 5.78 vs 6.39 (I-C vs placebo), a difference of -0.61 that did not reach statistical significance (p=0.0895). Multiple pre-specified exploratory analyses — including exclusion of a single outlier, extending symptom measurement to Day 1, and baseline-adjusted TSS — yielded statistically significant findings in favour of iota-carrageenan, though these require cautious interpretation as they were unplanned post-hoc analyses conducted after unblinding.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Day-by-day TSS values (Days 1-10 individual means with SE) are reported in Figure 2 only and could not be numerically extracted. Coronavirus NL63 and OC43 viral load data described only as '>94% reduction' without per-arm numeric means; not extractable. Duration-of-cold log-rank p-value not reported numerically. The paper reports 90.2% vs 72.0% reduction in HRV/HEV viral load as percentage change, which is derived from adjusted log means in Table 6.

summary: This open-label non-randomized comparative study conducted in Russia evaluated intranasal recombinant interferon alpha-2b (Interferal, 10^5 IU twice daily) and oral beta-D-glucan (Glucaferon, 2 capsules twice daily) versus standard symptomatic therapy (vasoconstrictor drops, Miramistine irrigation, Furacilin gargle) for 7 days in 114 adults with acute viral nasopharyngitis (60% rhinovirus). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) Study has no explicit randomization — described as a comparative study with group allocation by treatment; classified as non-randomized-comparative. 2) Arm_id assignment: arm_id=1=interferon (primary intervention), arm_id=2=beta-D-glucan, arm_id=3=standard therapy (usual_care/control), arm_id=4=healthy controls (no ANP, no treatment). 3) Symptom score data appear primarily in regression model equations (Y=intercept + slope*t) and in figures (Figures 4-7), not in tables with raw means/SDs per timepoint — day 1 intercept values extracted from regression equation constants; day 7 values calculated by substituting t=7 into models; these are model-predicted not empirical means. 4) IL-1beta and IL-1ra data (Table 1) only reported for healthy controls (Group 1) vs all ANP patients at baseline (Group 2 = all 114 ANP combined, not separated by treatment arm); day 7 arm-level cytokine data are only in figures (Figure 3) with no numeric values. 5) No per-arm SDs reported for symptom scores. 6) The between-group p-values for symptom scores are only stated as p<0.05 for regression coefficients, not as direct between-arm comparisons. 7) Illness duration reduction by 2 days stated narratively without supporting raw data. 8) Note: group 2 in Table 1 (n used for cytokine baseline) refers to all 114 ANP patients combined, not only the standard therapy group (38 patients labeled group 2 in treatment allocation). 9) The study drug Glucaferon is an oral (not nasal) preparation; included because paper evaluates it alongside an intranasal interferon spray as treatment for respiratory viral infection.

summary: This open-label, non-randomized four-arm comparative study enrolled 146 outpatients in Russia (2016-2019) with acute respiratory infections (within 48h of symptom onset) and comorbid seasonal allergic rhinitis in remission, comparing intranasal IFN-gamma drops, combined rectal+nasal IFN-alpha2b with antioxidants, oral pidotimod, and oral tilorone over 7-10 days. All four treatments produced significant daily reductions in a composite 15-symptom clinical score, with pidotimod achieving the lowest symptom burden by day 7 (statistically significantly better than all other arms, p<0.001), though baseline symptom severity was higher in the tilorone arm, complicating cross-arm comparisons. No adverse events were observed in any arm; the study was not placebo-controlled and lacked randomization, limiting causal conclusions.

summary: This double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (ACCROS-I) tested intranasal chlorpheniramine maleate (CPM) spray added to early multidrug standard of care versus placebo in 101 outpatients with mild-to-moderate PCR/antigen-confirmed COVID-19 in Honduras. At Day 7, the CPM group showed greater percent reductions in both Daily Symptoms Score (−18.8 ± 9.3%) and Visual Analogue Scale (−8.6 ± 5.1%) compared to placebo (p < 0.05), and had significantly lower proportions of patients reporting ageusia (p = 0.01), cough (p = 0.03), and nasal congestion (p = 0.02). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports two studies: ACCROS-I (RCT, n=101) and ACCROS-II (retrospective cohort, n=660); extraction focused on ACCROS-I RCT. Key quantitative data for the placebo arm's DSS and VAS Δ% values are not reported in the text body; only the CPM arm's Δ% ± SD is given. Per-arm event counts for binary secondary outcomes (ageusia, cough, nasal congestion) are not reported in the text — only Chi-squared statistics and p-values given; anosmia proportions are reported as percentages only (CPM 4.9%, PLB 15%). All detailed tables (Tables 1–4) are in supplementary files that were not accessible. Figures 1 and 2 contain primary and secondary outcome data respectively but numeric values are only available as described above. ACCROS-II retrospective data: 660 patients (330 CPM+SoC, 330 SoC); individual symptom durations reported as 3–5 days shorter in CPM+SoC cohort (p<0.001) but exact means/SDs not provided in text body — data appear only in Figure 4. Unequal randomization (61 vs 40) is unexplained. Chi-squared statistics reported: ageusia X²=6.69 p=0.01; cough X²=4.62 p=0.03; nasal congestion X²=4.64 p=0.02; anosmia X²=3.03 p=0.08. Duration of treatment was reported as approximately 10 days (CPM: 10.5 ± 0.5 days, PLB: 10.6 ± 0.5 days) based on compliance reporting, though the protocol stated 7-day primary endpoint.

The intervention group demonstrated significantly faster and more complete symptom resolution for sore throat, cough/mucus, and nasal congestion by Days 3 and 7 (all p<0.05), with complete recovery rates at Day 7 substantially higher for nasal congestion (31.1% vs 3.4%) and sore throat (26.2% vs 3.4%); no adverse events were reported in either group. Patient satisfaction scores were also significantly higher in the active treatment group (overall mean 4.03 vs 3.69, p<0.001), though the trial relied entirely on subjective Likert-scale symptom outcomes, included no virological endpoints, and was registered retrospectively nearly two years after completion.

No virological endpoints (viral load, PCR clearance) were reported — all efficacy outcomes are patient-reported symptom severity. 4. Day 1 is described as assessment on Day 1 after treatment initiation (not baseline); baseline (Day 0) symptom data not presented in tables. 8. The intervention combines nasal spray + mouth spray + mouthwash (not a single product); arm labeled accordingly. 9. Satisfaction sub-domain t-scores reported but CIs not given. 10. 1-month post-discharge follow-up mentioned for safety only; no efficacy data at that timepoint.

summary: This open-label, non-randomized comparative study tested intranasal interferon alpha-2b (VIFERON ointment or gel) combined with rectal interferon alpha-2b suppositories versus PPE alone for COVID-19 prevention in 150 Russian ambulance healthcare workers over one month. summary: This feasibility RCT randomized 102 adults to prophylactic iota-carrageenan nasal spray or saline placebo three times daily for 8 weeks to prevent upper respiratory tract infections, with a separate non-randomized observational control group (n=42) recording symptoms only.
