summary: This single-arm, open-label, before-and-after pilot study evaluated 0.4% povidone-iodine (PVP-I) nasal spray in 12 Thai adults with culture-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal infection, measuring viable viral titers by TCID50 culture at baseline, 3 minutes, and 4 hours after a single treatment. At 3 minutes post-spray, the median viral titer was essentially unchanged from baseline (3.5 vs 3.4 log TCID50/mL; P=0.162), with only a median 0.1-log reduction, and at 4 hours the titer remained similar to baseline (2.8 log TCID50/mL; P=0.704 vs 3-minute value). The authors concluded that 0.4% PVP-I nasal spray demonstrated poor in vivo virucidal activity against SARS-CoV-2 and is unlikely to reduce transmission; no adverse effects were observed.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT tested an iota-carrageenan (0.17%) nasal spray administered 4 times daily for 21 days as post-exposure prophylaxis against SARS-CoV-2 in 394 unvaccinated healthcare workers managing hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Argentina. RT-PCR-confirmed symptomatic COVID-19 occurred significantly less often in the iota-carrageenan arm (2/196, 1.0%) than in the placebo arm (10/198, 5.0%), yielding an OR of 0.19 (95% CI 0.05–0.77, p=0.03) and an absolute risk reduction of 4% (95% CI 0.6–7.4%). Adverse events were mild and did not differ between groups, supporting both efficacy and safety of iota-carrageenan nasal spray for COVID-19 prevention in high-exposure healthcare settings.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports relative risk reduction (79.8%, 95% CI 5.3–95.4) and absolute risk reduction (4%, 95% CI 0.6–7.4) in addition to the OR; the RRR CI is wide and the raw RR value is not explicitly stated (only calculable from events/totals as approximately 0.202). The Kaplan-Meier survival plot (Figure 2) contains time-to-event data that could not be extracted numerically as values are only in the figure. Six participants excluded post-randomization (before the 394 ITT population) due to baseline symptoms; these were subtracted from the 400 enrolled. The overall age SD of 9.0 is approximate — the paper states '38.5±9 years' without specifying the exact SD digit.

summary: This open-label, non-randomized comparative study tested a nasal spray containing alpha-cyclodextrin (0.20%) and hydroxytyrosol (3.80%) for prevention of SARS-CoV-2 infection over 30 days in 149 healthy healthcare-worker volunteers at Near East University (Cyprus), compared to 76 controls who chose not to use the spray. None of the 225 participants in either arm became RT-qPCR positive or seroconverted during the study period, resulting in zero events in both arms and precluding any between-group statistical comparison. The study provides preliminary safety data (no adverse events in spray users) and in vitro evidence of antiviral activity, but its non-randomized design, open-label assignment, and zero-event primary outcome severely limit causal inference.

summary: This randomized double-blind crossover allergen challenge trial (N=41) tested a carrageenan- and sorbitol-containing nasal spray (Coldamaris Akut/CS) versus 0.5% saline solution (SS) in adults with moderate-to-severe seasonal allergic rhinitis during controlled grass pollen exposure. The primary endpoint (subjective nasal congestion symptom score change at 2-4h post-treatment) was not met (mean difference CS vs SS = 0.02, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.24, p>0.05). However, CS significantly improved objective nasal airflow compared to SS at 6h (mean difference 54.29 mL/s, 95% CI 2.92-105.66, p=0.04) and significantly reduced nasal secretion within the CS arm (−1.00 g, −25%, p=0.003), while the SS reduction was not significant; note that this study tests the carrageenan spray in an allergen (not viral) challenge model.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial tests the spray against allergen-induced rhinitis (grass pollen challenge), NOT against a respiratory viral infection directly; the carrageenan component has antiviral properties but virus infection is not an endpoint here. The trial is included as a decongestant/barrier-agent trial. Nasal airflow absolute values at pre-treatment and 6h timepoints are only presented in figures (Figure 6) — numeric means and SDs are not given in tables; only the between-group difference (54.29 mL/s) is stated in text. TNSS, TOSS, and TRSS numeric data are not provided in tables ('data not shown'). The nasal secretion between-group difference p-value at 6h is described as significant (lower bound CI >0) but exact values for the between-group difference are only shown in Figure 7; exact p-value for between-group comparison not stated. Within-arm p-values for nasal secretion change: CS p=0.003, SS p=0.137. The crossover design means per-arm n_randomized values are the same (all 41 participants received both treatments). Two participants missed visit 4 (second treatment block) due to AEs — one from each first-treatment arm; the nasal airflow analysis used n=38. No per-arm baseline demographics are provided as this is a crossover study.

summary: This open-label pilot RCT tested a proprietary nicotinic cholinergic agonist nasal spray plus oral drops (CA, Niccovid®) added to standard of care versus standard of care alone in 80 Colombian outpatients (40 per arm) with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, as a treatment for COVID-19 symptoms over 15 days. Among 10 symptoms assessed, CA was associated with statistically significant OR reductions for cough (OR 0.57, p=0.017), ageusia (OR 0.15, p=0.037), and anosmia (OR 0.65, p=0.049), with non-significant trends favoring CA for dyspnea, muscle fatigue, headache, general malaise, fever, and nasal congestion. The trial has major methodological limitations including open-label design, undisclosed randomization method, baseline imbalances, and no per-arm raw event counts reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. No per-arm raw event counts or means/SDs are reported for any outcome — only ORs with 95% CIs and p-values are provided in Table 2. Graphical data (Figures 1-10 showing expected impact on symptom duration in days) are not quantitatively extractable from text. The OR methodology is described as reflecting 'expected impact' on symptom days but the statistical construction is non-standard and not fully described (unclear whether ORs represent longitudinal symptom-day ORs or cross-sectional prevalence at end). The N in AE table for nasal spray side effects sums to 35 unique patients appearing to experience at least one AE out of 40 (91.4% had nasal itching = 32/35 not 40), suggesting a subset of intervention patients reported. Arm 1 (intervention) had mean age 45.2y vs. arm 2 (control) 53.7y, and substantially different comorbidity profiles and SOC medication use, raising baseline imbalance concerns. No primary outcome was pre-specified.

summary: This Egyptian double-blind RCT tested combined nasal and oropharyngeal sprays containing povidone-iodine 0.5% and glycyrrhizic acid 2.5 mg/ml (6 times daily) versus placebo in 200 adults with early PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and negative chest CT. Treatment significantly accelerated PCR negativity (99% vs 90% by day 10), shortened time to symptom resolution (7.6 vs 8.9 days, p=0.008), and dramatically reduced household transmission to contacts (4% vs 69% PCR-confirmed, p<0.0001). All primary and secondary outcomes showed statistically significant benefit in the treatment group, with no serious adverse effects in the treatment arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 note: the abstract states 'day 4: 70 vs. 99% PCR positive' and the results text states '30 vs. 1% PCR negative' on day 4; these are consistent (70 positive = 30 negative in treatment arm; 99 positive = 1 negative in placebo arm). Day 7 abstract states '20 vs. 65% PCR positive' but Table 2 and results text state '21/79 vs. 65/35', consistent. The number of contacts in placebo group is reported as 277 in Table 1 but as 227 in Table 2 — this discrepancy is present in the paper; Table 2 figures (227) used for outcome calculations as they are tied to the outcome data. N for anosmia/ageusia subgroups inferred from Table 1 (arm 1: anosmia n=59, ageusia n=56; arm 2: anosmia n=64, ageusia n=53). CI for anosmia recovery in text states '[4.6:6.9] for anosmia and [4.4:6.9] for ageusia' as CI around the mean for the treatment arm, while Table 3 shows [4.8:6.4] for smell and [4.8:6.5] for taste — used Table 3 values as they are more specific. The between-group CI for DSD is reported as [-2.2:-0.4] so mean difference calculated as -1.3 (7.6-8.9). The paper does not report between-group effect sizes (RR, OR) for binary outcomes; only chi-square p-values are given. summary: This open-label RCT in 90 hospitalized male military servicemen with uncomplicated ARIs compared intranasal IFN-α2b gel plus rectal suppositories vs rectal suppositories alone vs umifenovir (active comparator) over 5 days with 3-month follow-up. The text is heavily garbled with encoding artifacts (Cyrillic rendered as Latin look-alikes) but sufficient content was extractable from tables and English-language sections. Table 3 IFN data are reported as median; 25th–75th percentile; min–max format — extracted medians and IQR bounds. Arm labeling note: arm_id=1 is the combination (rectal+intranasal) intervention, arm_id=2 is rectal suppositories only, arm_id=3 is umifenovir. IFN-γ plasma concentrations and spontaneous/induced IFN-γ production data from Table 3 were not separately extracted as individual outcome objects to stay within output limits; these showed baseline IFN-γ production was heterogeneous across groups (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.005). Induced IFN-α ex vivo production data appear primarily in figures (Figs 2, 3, 4) with only partial numeric data in text; quantitative arm-level numbers for this outcome were therefore not extractable. summary: This Phase 1 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 48 healthy Australian adults tested intranasal egg-derived anti-SARS-CoV-2 RBD immunoglobulin Y (IgY) drops at single ascending doses (2, 4, 8 mg) and multiple daily doses (6, 12, 24 mg/day for 14 days) as prophylaxis against SARS-CoV-2. No formal statistical comparisons of infection outcomes were conducted, as this was a Phase 1 safety trial in healthy volunteers without viral challenge.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a Phase 1 safety/tolerability/PK trial only — there are no infection incidence or efficacy outcomes. No primary efficacy endpoint was assessed and no between-group statistical comparisons for any clinical outcome were reported. Placebo arm was split across Part 1 (n=6) and Part 2 (n=6); arm_id=7 represents the combined placebo group (n=12 randomized, n=11 completed). Part 2 arm labels (2 mg TID, 4 mg TID, 8 mg TID) correspond to daily doses of 6, 12, 24 mg respectively. Demographics table notes arm_id 7 placebo demographics separately for Part 1 and Part 2 but combined values for overall placebo are not reported together; per-arm demographics for placebo Part 1: mean age 22.7 (SD 2.34), 100% female; placebo Part 2: mean age 25.3 (SD 6.41), 66.7% female. Cytokine data (outcome_id 4) are only partially described in text with no per-arm quantitative values reported; detailed data are only in Supplementary Figure S3 (not available). The hamster efficacy data showed no in vivo efficacy but this is a preclinical finding and not extracted as a human trial outcome. Pairwise AE comparisons between active doses not reported. Note: Table 2 header describes Part 2 doses as '2 mg TID', '4 mg TID', '8 mg TID' which equal total daily doses of 6 mg, 12 mg, 24 mg respectively.

summary: This Phase III double-blind RCT tested 0.5% povidone-iodine nasal spray (Nasodine) versus saline nasal spray placebo as a treatment for the common cold in 260 Australian adults with recent-onset symptoms. Nasodine showed a consistent directional benefit across all WURSS-21 outcomes; the key secondary endpoint (Global Severity Score) showed a 12.6% benefit over saline that approached but did not reach statistical significance in the ITT population (p=0.054), while the QoL/functional impairment subscale was statistically significant (16.1% benefit, p=0.041). Post hoc subgroup analyses showed substantially larger and statistically significant effects in subjects with stronger symptoms, confirmed viral infections, or treatment initiated within 24 hours of symptom onset (up to ~40% benefit), but these were unplanned analyses subject to multiplicity concerns.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: LSM values represent least squares means from a general linear model (GLM) with Day 1 baseline as covariate and treatment/site as factors. Between-group effect values are derived from the paper's stated 'Difference LSM' columns (placebo minus Nasodine), recast as Nasodine minus placebo (negative = Nasodine better). The paper states '22.5%' benefit for VES GSS in Table 2 but the abstract and text state '23.0%' — the table LSM calculation (10.23/45.56=22.4%) is consistent with the table figure of 22.5%; the abstract figure of 23.0% appears to be a rounding variant. Time to Cessation of Shedding (TCS) result described as 'three days sooner for Nasodine' but individual arm medians not provided in text; only p=0.42 stated. Individual item-level WURSS-21 data appear only in Figures 5 and 6 and were not extracted. Post hoc 'Time to Alleviation of Illness' (TAI) endpoint (Nasodine 3.4 days vs placebo 4.0 days, p=0.007) not captured as a separate outcome as definition and derivation were not fully specified. n_completed for each arm estimated as n_randomized minus n_withdrawn (5 total withdrawals: 2 Nasodine + 2 Nasodine AE = stated as 2 AE, 1 placebo AE; paper states 'three subjects withdrawn due to adverse events' but also 'five withdrawn total').

summary: This 3-arm open-label RCT (n=54 ITT) tested Sentinox (hypochlorous acid nasal spray, 0.005% HClO) administered 3x/day (STX-3) or 5x/day (STX-5) as add-on to standard care vs standard care alone in mild COVID-19 outpatients over 5 days. The primary endpoint (viral load reduction at any treatment day in the full ITT population) was not met, with STX-3 showing a non-significant 1.02 log10 reduction vs control (p=0.14); in a pre-specified subgroup with medium baseline viral loads (Ct 20-30), STX-3 achieved a significant 2.01 log10 reduction (p=0.016), and the proportion achieving viral negativization by day 5 was significantly higher with STX-3 than controls (RR 1.62, 95% CI 1.23-2.15 for Ct>40 cutoff). The spray was safe and well-tolerated, with notably fewer serious adverse events (disease progression/hospitalization) in the treatment groups (2.8%) versus controls (16.7%), though this was an unplanned observation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm raw viral load change-from-baseline means and SDs at each timepoint are not reported in tables — data appear only in figures (Figures 2 and 3) and thus result_source set to 'not_reported' for individual arm viral load change results. Exact event counts for negativization (Ct>40 and Ct>35) are not given numerically — only percentages are stated; events were not calculable precisely because the denominators imply fractional events (e.g. 29% of 17 = 4.93), so events fields left null. P-value for overall treatment effect reported as p=0.95 (no significant overall group difference). The 'any AE' p-value reported as p>0.99 (verbatim). The pooled treatment arms comparison for serious AEs (2.8% vs 16.7%) is a post-hoc descriptive comparison noted in the discussion, not a formal statistical test. The between_group_effects for the Ct>40 and Ct>35 negativization outcomes use Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel RRs as reported. Arm_id=1 (STX-3) is the primary intervention because it showed statistically significant results; arm_id=2 (STX-5) is secondary intervention; arm_id=3 is control. Active comparator pairwise comparison between STX-3 and STX-5 not included per output management rules. In vitro virucidal data not extracted as it is not a clinical outcome.

summary: This Italian prospective open-label controlled trial (RENAISSANCE) tested a hypertonic seawater nasal spray (Tonimer Lab Panthexyl 800, containing seawater, xylitol, panthenol, and lactic acid) as a treatment for confirmed SARS-CoV-2 (Omicron) infection in 108 adult outpatients with mild or asymptomatic COVID-19. summary: This two-phase Chinese single-center RCT evaluated lentinan nasal drops (a β-glucan immunomodulator) as treatment for mild Omicron COVID-19 infection. In Phase 1 (n=24, dose-escalation), the 100 µg/day dose significantly shortened RT-PCR viral shedding time versus standard care (7.75 vs 13.41 days, p=0.013). In Phase 2 (n=70, placebo-controlled), 100 µg/day lentinan significantly increased antigen negative conversion rates at day 5 (36.2% vs 13.0%, p=0.044) and day 7 (70.2% vs 60.9%, p=0.013), with shorter median time to antigen negativity (7 vs 8 days, p=0.029), but no significant differences in clinical symptom improvement were observed between groups.

Phase 1 had 12 patients in each arm (lentinan vs control), but the 12 lentinan patients were split across 3 dose subgroups (50/75/100 µg, ~4 each) — exact n per subgroup not explicitly stated, inferred as ~4 each. 2. Phase 2 randomized 74 patients at 2:1; 4 excluded (2 missing data, 2 withdrew), leaving 70 analyzed (47 lentinan, 23 placebo). The 2:1 ratio implies ~49-50 lentinan and ~24-25 placebo randomized. 3. CI values for median antigen conversion time are labeled 'CI%' in the paper and may represent confidence intervals rather than IQR — extracted as ci_95_low/high. 4. Some symptom data in Table 4 use different denominators at day 5 vs day 1/7 (e.g. 'N=47' stated but some cells show denominators implying 43 for day 5 fatigue — used 47 throughout as per table header). 5. The paper states the arm 1 nucleic acid shedding time in Table 1 as 9.67±2.64 but this represents the combined lentinan group (all 3 doses, n=12). 6. Phase 1 control group had a slightly different value reported in two places: Table 1 says 13.41±3.8 and text says 13.42±3.8 — used 13.41 as in Table 1. 7. Kaplan-Meier curves shown in Figure 4B/4C but numeric HR not reported — p-value only extracted. 8. summary: This single-arm, open-label study in 10 RT-PCR-confirmed COVID-19 patients in South India assessed the effect of 7-day topical 1% povidone-iodine (intranasal cotton-bud application 0.3 mL QID + oral gargle 25 mL QID) on SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR cycle threshold (Ct) values sampled from nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal sites at Hours 0, 2, and 4 on Days 0, 3, 6, and 9. Higher Ct values (lower viral load) were observed at Hour 2 post-PVP-I for most samples, hinting at transient virucidal activity, but no consistent statistically significant within-day differences were found across the study period.

summary: This open-label, blank-controlled non-randomized study evaluated SA58 Nasal Spray — a broad-spectrum anti-SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibody spray — for prevention of COVID-19 (Omicron variants) among medical personnel working in COVID-19 hospitals in Hohhot, China, October–November 2022. Over 30 days of daily RT-PCR monitoring, 7 of 27,103 person-days in the drug group resulted in infection (0.026%) versus 128 of 110,441 person-days in the control group (0.116%), yielding a calculated effectiveness of 77.7%. However, the study's non-randomized self-selected design with open-label allocation introduces high risk of confounding, limiting causal interpretation of these findings.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This is a non-randomized, consent-based allocation study — no randomization occurred; arm assignment was purely by participant willingness to use SA58. 2) Person-days (not participants) were used as the denominator for the primary outcome (rate per person-day); individual-level N in the control arm is not explicitly reported — only person-days (110,441) and cases (128). 3) The SA58 drug group had 3,368 enrolled participants but only 1,736 reported medication info via APP (used for safety); effectiveness denominators use person-days not person-counts. 4) Total enrolled was 6,662; 1,596 were excluded after leaving Hohhot within 2 days, leaving 5,066 in the effectiveness analysis set — but exact breakdown by arm is not given as person-counts. 5) AE percentages reported by symptom type (rhinorrhea 14.5%, dryness 9.6%, sneezing 8.7%, etc.) refer to percent of 1,736 APP reporters, but exact N per AE not stated — only percentages in figures. 6) The paper states effectiveness of 77.7% but does not provide CI or p-value for this estimate. 7) No AE data reported for the control group. 8) Baseline demographics (age, sex) reported only for the 1,736 APP-reporting drug arm participants, not the full drug group or control group.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Treatment effect on viral burden increased monotonically with age; statistically significant reductions in vAUCd1-8 were observed from 45 Y+ onward (p=0.017 to p=0.005), with the largest effect in 65 Y+ (-7.3 log10 copies/mL×Day, p=0.005). summary: This double-blind RCT evaluated astodrimer sodium (SPL7013) 1% nasal spray (4x/day for 7 days) versus saline placebo in 222 non-hospitalised adults with confirmed COVID-19 in the UK. In the full mITT population (n=197), astodrimer reduced SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal viral burden (vAUCd1-8) by 1.2 log10 copies/mL×Day versus placebo, but this did not reach statistical significance (p=0.344); however, statistically significant and clinically meaningful reductions were observed in participants aged 45 years and older, with the largest effect in the 65 Y+ subgroup (-7.3 log10 copies/mL×Day, p=0.005). Astodrimer also accelerated viral clearance (p=0.035 for clearance rate), increased the proportion achieving RT-qPCR negativity by Day 8 in older age groups, and reduced the proportion experiencing loss of smell/taste, with a well-tolerated safety profile.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: LSM values (not raw means) are reported for the primary vAUCd1-8 outcome; these are ANCOVA-adjusted least-squares means with SE, not arithmetic means with SD — stored in se field accordingly. Per-arm N for the safety population (n_analyzed for AEs): arm 1=109, arm 2=113. Total AE count across both arms combined was 31 (14%); per-arm breakdown of 'any AE' events not explicitly stated in text. Anosmia/ageusia and most FLU-PRO domain results reported primarily in supplementary tables (S6-S10) and figures not available in full text — specific per-arm event counts for anosmia/ageusia not extractable from main text. Throat domain recovery (80% vs 51.4%, p=0.031) reported for 55Y+ but denominator N not given in text. Daily viral load values are only in supplementary Tables S4-S5 and figures — not extracted. Peak viral load and time-to-peak viral load results are in supplementary Table S2-S3 and figures — not extracted. The 40 Y+ subgroup Fisher's exact p-value for negative RT-qPCR is reported (p=0.097) but HR p-value=0.180 — HR not statistically significant. Outcome 16 anosmia: numerical proportions by arm not stated in main text, only noted as 'consistently lower' with significance reached in 55Y+ and 65Y+ subgroups per Figure 8. Funder (Starpharma) had substantial involvement in study design, analysis, and reporting — conflict of interest noted.

summary: This double-blind RCT (n=50) compared intranasal xylitol spray (11% xylitol with grapefruit seed extract) versus isotonic saline spray for 14 days in adult outpatients with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection within 3 days of symptom onset in the Dominican Republic. No statistically significant differences were found between groups in VAS symptom scores (p=0.124), daily symptom scores (p=0.448), or olfactory function (p=0.667); both treatments performed similarly for symptom resolution and neither group required hospitalization. Notably, xylitol was associated with higher rates of nasal congestion (Day 4: 73.1% vs 41.7%, p=0.025; Day 7: 50.0% vs 17.4%, p=0.017), and persistent anosmia at Day 28 was observed only in the saline group (2/24 vs 0/26), though this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.133).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. All quantitative VAS, DSS, and olfactory function results over time are presented only in figures (Figures 1-3) with no extractable numeric values in the text or tables; only the overall repeated-measures ANOVA p-values are reported. The age reported (40.14 ± 2.16) uses SEM not SD per the results section statement ('Data in graphs are mean ± SEM'). Baseline demographics are not broken down by arm. summary: This double-blind phase IIb RCT (n=80) tested nitric oxide nasal spray (NONS) versus saline placebo in UK adults with mild, confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, administered 5-6 times daily for 9 days. NONS was associated with significantly greater reductions in log10 SARS-CoV-2 RNA at days 2 (mean difference -1.21, 95% CI -2.07 to -0.35, p=0.01) and day 4 (mean difference -1.21, 95% CI -2.19 to -0.24, p=0.02), with the AUC treatment difference from baseline to day 6 also statistically significant (mean difference -5.22, 95% CI -9.14 to -1.31, p=0.001); the day 6 timepoint alone did not reach significance (p=0.069). A higher proportion of NONS respondents reported feeling better during treatment (46.7% vs 8%), though the questionnaire return rate was low and unbalanced between arms.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm viral load means and SDs at individual timepoints (days 1-6) are only available in Figure 1 (not tabulated in text) — raw arm-level mean/SD data cannot be extracted for individual timepoints. The between-group treatment differences at days 2, 4, and 6 are explicitly stated in the text with CIs and p-values and were extracted verbatim. The AUC mean changes (-10.17 NONS, -4.95 placebo) are stated in the text and used as the arm-level AUC results; it is unclear if these are strictly AUC values or cumulative change values. Only 40/80 participants returned the symptom questionnaire (15 NONS, 25 placebo), creating high risk of response bias for the symptom outcome. BMI was significantly imbalanced between arms at baseline (p=0.034). The paper is a correspondence/letter format and does not report allocation concealment or full CONSORT flow. No per-arm SD or SE reported for any viral load outcome.

summary: This double-blind RCT evaluated inhaled zanamivir (10 mg oral inhalation + 6.4 mg intranasal spray, 2x or 4x daily for 5 days) versus placebo for treatment of influenza A and B infection in 1256 adults with influenza-like illness. Both zanamivir dosing regimens significantly reduced the median time to alleviation of major symptoms by 1 day (6 vs. 7 days; p=0.012 and p=0.014) in the ITT population, with greater benefit in febrile patients, those treated within 30 hours of onset, and high-risk patients. Zanamivir also significantly reduced symptom severity scores, disturbed sleep, time to return to normal activities, and use of relief medications, with an adverse event profile comparable to placebo.

summary: This document is a comprehensive drug review/monograph summarizing the pharmacology, therapeutic efficacy, and safety of inhaled zanamivir (a neuraminidase inhibitor) administered as dry powder inhalation (10 mg twice daily for 5 days) with or without adjunctive intranasal spray (6.4 mg two or four times daily) for the treatment and prophylaxis of influenza A and B in adults, high-risk patients (including those with asthma/COPD), and children aged 5-12 years, across multiple randomized double-blind placebo-controlled phase II and III trials. For treatment, zanamivir significantly reduced median time to symptom alleviation by approximately 1-2.5 days versus placebo across all populations, with statistically significant effects in influenza-confirmed patients (p≤0.05 to p<0.001); for prophylaxis, the drug demonstrated 67-96% protective efficacy in both challenge and community settings. The drug was generally well tolerated with an adverse event profile similar to placebo across both treatment and prophylaxis indications.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This source is a narrative drug review/monograph (Drugs journal), not a primary trial report. It summarizes results from multiple distinct RCTs and pooled analyses without always providing per-arm raw counts needed for pooling. Outcomes extracted represent summary data reported from individual trials (as named in the text) and pooled analyses. Adverse event percentages by arm were reported as proportions of total N (zanamivir n=2289, placebo n=1520 in treatment trials; zanamivir n=1063, placebo n=744 in prophylaxis trials) but individual event counts were not given. Several outcomes (community-based post-exposure prophylaxis trial, nursing home prophylaxis data, some symptom severity data) contain insufficient quantitative data for full extraction and are described only narratively. Prophylactic efficacy in the human challenge studies is reported as overall protective efficacy percentage without individual arm proportions for shedding/infection. The Monto et al. phase II trial data were only available for the ITT population. Table III data were extracted for the most informative trials. The delayed treatment human challenge arm (n=38, starting 50h post-inoculation) data for AUCv (75% reduction, p<0.05) and median viral shedding duration (1 vs 2 days, p<0.05) were not included as full outcome entries due to limited quantitative detail. Nursing home prophylaxis comparison with rimantadine (zanamivir 2.9% vs rimantadine 7.4% influenza A, p=0.038, n=238 vs 244) not included as a separate outcome as it is an active comparator study rather than placebo-controlled.

summary: This pooled analysis of four randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled human challenge trials tested intranasal zanamivir (GG167), a neuraminidase inhibitor, against experimental influenza A (H1N1) infection in 166 susceptible healthy adults for both prevention and treatment. For prophylaxis, GG167 was 82% effective in preventing laboratory-confirmed infection and 95% effective in preventing febrile illness (P<0.001 vs placebo). For early treatment (begun ~26-32 hours after viral inoculation), GG167 reduced peak viral titers by approximately 2.0 log10, duration of viral shedding by a median of 3 days, and febrile illness frequency by 84% (all P<0.05), with twice-daily dosing as effective as six-times-daily dosing.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper pools four separate trials (n=48, 56, 31, 31) conducted at two sites. Adverse event table reports prophylaxis GG167 (n=63) and treatment GG167 (n=54) as separate groups vs combined placebo (n=49) — these totals exceed the 117 GG167 participants reported in demographics, suggesting some overlap or different denominators. Table 3 (prophylaxis) has merged/garbled cells with per-row subject counts partially missing; arm-level n values (16, 10, 10, 8 for drops and spray groups) are partially inferable from table rows but not fully explicit. The combined early treatment group data (n=31 GG167, n=26 placebo) in Table 5 represents the pooled day-1 treatment arms from Trials 1 and 2 — these include both 6x/day and 2x/day dosing schedules combined; individual arm n values for Trial 2 arms (16mg 6x/day at 26h and 2x/day at 32h) appear to sum to ~20 but exact per-arm n is not stated. Symptom score data from Figure 1 and Figure 3 are available only as graphs. Table 5 notes placebo group used for both early and delayed treatment comparisons (same n=26 across both; Day 2 delayed treatment placebo AUC 5.2±4.9 is a subset period of the same patients). The between_group_effects median difference for duration of shedding is calculated from median values (not means); this is an approximation. Overall infection efficacy 82% stated verbatim in abstract/results; shedding efficacy 96% stated verbatim. Pairwise comparisons among GG167 dose subgroups are not reported.

summary: This 4-arm RCT tested intranasal zanamivir, inhaled zanamivir, and combined inhaled-plus-intranasal zanamivir versus placebo as 5-day post-exposure prophylaxis in 575 community members who had close contact with influenza-like illness index cases. Intranasal zanamivir alone was ineffective (OR 0.90, p=0.855), and the combined route showed no significant benefit (OR 0.52, p=0.247), but inhaled zanamivir reduced symptomatic influenza from 6% on placebo to 2% (OR 0.27, p=0.058), approaching but not reaching statistical significance.

summary: This large UK pragmatic RCT (n=13,799) tested a pH-buffering gel-based nasal spray (Vicks First Defence), a saline nasal spray, and a digital behavioural intervention against usual care for prevention and treatment of mixed respiratory tract infections in adults with comorbidities or recurrent illness over six winter months. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled human challenge trial tested intranasal 4',6-dichloroflavan (5% suspension, 5x/day for 26 doses) against experimental rhinovirus type 9 infection in 49 seronegative healthy adult volunteers at the MRC Common Cold Unit. Dichloroflavan did not significantly reduce clinical colds (28% vs 33% placebo), virological infection rates (76% vs 71% for any evidence of infection), or total symptom scores or nasal secretion weights, and there was a non-significant trend toward increased severity and rhinorrhoea in the treated group. None of the differences achieved statistical significance, and the trial was acknowledged to be underpowered to detect all but large protective effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Continuous outcome data (total clinical scores, mean daily clinical scores, nasal secretion weights, and daily virus excretion proportions) are stated to exist but presented only in Figure 1 and not tabulated numerically — extracted as not_reported. Table 1 provides complete per-arm, per-stratum counts for binary outcomes. Two volunteers of the original 59 withdrew before completion for reasons unrelated to the study; of the remaining 57, only 49 were challenged with virus (8 received saline due to high baseline antibody titres >= 1:64 and were excluded from efficacy analysis). The arm_id=1 dichloroflavan group: 8 males, 17 females, mean age 29.36 ± 8.91 years; arm_id=2 placebo group: 7 males, 17 females, mean age 31.04 ± 11.61 years. Percent female for arm 1 calculated as 17/25=68%; for arm 2 as 17/24=70.8%. The nasal secretion weight difference on day 5 reached p=0.044 (two-tailed) favoring more rhinorrhoea in the dichloroflavan group; days 3, 4, and 6 were non-significant (p=0.48, 0.72, 0.32 respectively). Treatment duration: 26 doses at 5/day = 5.2 days total (5 doses pre-challenge + 21 post-challenge).

risk_of_bias.key_concern: 168/268 infants (63%) were excluded from efficacy analyses due to absent RSV circulation in season 3 (COVID-19 pandemic), reducing the mITT to only 94 of the planned 408 infants and substantially reducing statistical power, though early stopping for futility per pre-specified interim analysis mitigates reporting concerns.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Infants enrolled in season 3 (n=168) were excluded from efficacy analyses due to absent RSV circulation during COVID-19 pandemic; only seasons 1 and 2 (n=100 enrolled, n=94 mITT) contributed to primary analysis.
All four missing-data sensitivity analyses in the ITT population (N=100) showed aOR ranging 1.5-2.8 (none statistically significant), consistent with the primary mITT analysis.
Per-protocol analysis (16/42 [38.1%] palivizumab vs 11/44 [25.0%] placebo; aOR 1.9, 95% CI 0.6-6.3) consistent with primary mITT result.

summary: This double-blind RCT tested daily intranasal palivizumab (1 mg/mL, 50 µL per nostril) versus placebo saline drops for prevention of RSV infection in 268 late preterm infants (gestational age 32-35 weeks) in the Netherlands over three RSV seasons. The trial was stopped early for futility after a pre-specified interim analysis: in the mITT population (n=94, seasons 1-2 only), RSV infection occurred in 38.3% of the palivizumab arm versus 23.4% of placebo (aOR 2.2, 95% CI 0.7-6.5, p=0.14), with no statistically significant benefit and a non-significant trend toward more infections in the treated group. Daily intranasal palivizumab did not prevent RSV infection, with the most likely explanation being insufficient mucosal antibody half-life in the nasal cavity.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: SAE counts (22 palivizumab, 26 placebo) appear to reflect serious AEs in the full randomized safety population (N=134 per arm), while any AE percentage (16.4% and 19.4%) uses the same denominators — these likely represent the same counts (serious AEs). Wheezing outcomes (fraction of wheezing days, recurrent wheezing, physician-diagnosed wheeze) have data only in supplementary tables (S7-S10) not reproduced in the main paper text; the IRR of 1.2 (95% CI 0.8-1.7) is the only wheezing effect size in the main text. Follow-up duration not explicitly stated in weeks but was approximately one RSV season (~6 months, October to March). Treatment duration mean: 3.9 months (SD 1.1) in palivizumab arm, 3.7 months (SD 1.1) in placebo arm. The paper also reports a phase I safety crossover trial (Study A, n=20 adults) with no SAEs; this extraction focuses on the phase IIb efficacy trial (Study B) in infants. Non-medically attended RTI data (palivizumab 43/47 [91.5%], placebo 45/47 [95.7%]; OR 0.5, 95% CI 0.08-2.7; RD -4.3%, 95% CI -14.1 to 5.6) omitted from outcomes list to stay within size limits.

summary: This double-blind RCT tested intranasal recombinant interferon alpha-2 (HuIFN-alpha2) at 2.5x10^6 IU/day (twice-daily nasal spray) versus placebo for 12 days in 287 healthy working adults for prevention of naturally occurring respiratory viral infections. The trial was stopped early due to significant local intolerance: 44% of IFN recipients vs 15% of placebo recipients developed blood-tinged nasal mucus (p<0.001), and overall respiratory illness was actually more frequent in the IFN arm (44% vs 27%, p=0.004), driven largely by nasal irritation mimicking respiratory illness. Only 9 laboratory-documented viral infections occurred (6 IFN, 3 placebo), making efficacy assessment impossible, and no significant antiviral protection was demonstrated.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports episode counts rather than person-level infection counts for most outcomes (Table 1); events/total extracted assuming person-level counts match n in each arm as stated in the text for illness proportions (e.g., '44% of HuIFN' = ~62/142). The n_analyzed for mucosal exam outcomes (outcomes 9-10) is approximately one-third of each arm (rotating weekly exam sub-sample) but exact denominator not stated — percent only extracted. Blood-tinged mucus event counts back-calculated from stated percentages (44% x142=62; 15% x145=22; 34% x142=48; 11% x145=16) and marked as calculated. The placebo arm row in Table 1 appears garbled in the source ('40 3 0 1 1') — interpreted as 40 total respiratory illness episodes with 0 rhinovirus, 0 parainfluenza, 1 influenza B, 1 adenovirus based on context. P-values for blood-tinged mucus and any adverse symptom stated as 'P<0.001' and nasal dryness as 'P<0.005' — treated as threshold not exact values.

summary: This double-blind RCT tested intranasal recombinant human interferon alpha-2 (HuIFN-a2, 8.4×10^6 U/day) versus placebo spray for 28 consecutive days in 52 healthy adult volunteers as a prophylaxis strategy against respiratory viral infections. The primary finding was that HuIFN-a2 caused clinically and histologically significant nasal mucosal toxicity: 23% of recipients showed signs of mucosal irritation, 19% had moderate/severe epithelial inflammation with ulceration on biopsy, and 58% developed pronounced submucosal lymphocytic/mononuclear infiltrates — all significantly higher than placebo (p<0.001 for submucosal inflammation). The authors concluded that long-term intranasal HuIFN-a2 at this dosage is not a feasible prophylactic strategy due to unacceptable mucosal toxicity, although the histopathologic changes resolved within 8 weeks of stopping treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a safety/tolerability study; there was no planned efficacy (infection prevention) primary endpoint and no experimental viral challenge — volunteers were exposed to natural respiratory viruses during follow-up. The study was designed to assess histopathologic and symptomatic tolerance. Table 1 symptom counts are number of subjects reporting (not all subjects), with separate column for mean days/person. Table 2 contains some merged or ambiguous cell groupings (e.g. submucosal moderate n=3 and severe n=12 combined as 15 in the ± column header); these have been extracted as best as possible from the text. The n_any_ae for arm 1 (n=6) reflects clinical exam findings of mucosal irritation; the histologic abnormalities affected a larger proportion but are captured in separate outcome objects. Note: paper_id is inferred from journal/year/volume/page — not a DOI confirmed in the text. Placebo arm n_analyzed for histology is stated as 26 in Table 2 (includes two who did not complete 28 days). Mean symptomatic days for hoarseness in placebo reported as '<0.1' — extracted as 0.1 as a conservative upper bound.

summary: Three double-blind experimental rhinovirus challenge trials at the MRC Common Cold Unit tested three unrelated intranasal antiviral agents (SKF 40491, GL R9-338, and RP 19326) against matched placebo in healthy adult volunteers (n=8-13 per arm) using rhinovirus types 3 or 9. All three compounds reduced nasal virus shedding compared to placebo; the reductions were statistically significant for GL R9-338 (P<0.02) and RP 19326 (P<0.001), while SKF 40491 showed a trend but paradoxically worsened symptom scores (P<0.01), likely due to mucosal irritation. No compound produced a statistically significant reduction in clinical symptoms, though RP 19326 showed a trend toward symptom improvement.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Three separate parallel-group challenge trials are embedded in one paper; arms 1-2 = SKF 40491 trial (rhinovirus type 3); arms 3-4 = GL R9-338 trial (rhinovirus type 9); arms 5-6 = RP 19326 trial (rhinovirus type 9). A fourth compound (ICI 73,602) was tested in vitro only, not in volunteers. Table 3 also includes saline-challenge control subgroups for SKF and RP trials (not extracted as separate arms as they are not antiviral comparisons). The paper reports n_analyzed values as two numbers in parentheses (e.g. '10 (9)') — the first is total assessed, the second (in parentheses) appears to be the antibody-seronegative subset used for assessment; the larger value was used for n_completed/n_analyzed. Mean viral titer and mean clinical score data also appear in figures 1-3 but numerical values are also given in Table 3 (used here). Exact statistical method for p-values: Elston-Grizzle polynomial regression on repeated measures. The p-value for SKF 40491 symptom score (arm1 worse than arm2, P<0.01) is retained in between_group_effects with a positive mean_difference indicating treated group had higher (worse) score. No SDs reported for any outcome. Treatment duration in hours given (e.g. -20 to +84 hr for SKF) but total follow-up was 10 days plus ~18-day serology follow-up.

summary: This double-blind RCT evaluated F61, a recombinant human anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibody nasal spray (24 mg/0.8 mL), for prevention of COVID-19 (Omicron BA.5/BF.7) in healthy Chinese adults at risk of exposure during December 2022–January 2023. In 901 participants (450 per arm), 7-day daily dosing achieved a protective efficacy of 72.19% (95% CI 57.33–81.87%) compared with saline placebo, whereas a single dose was only protective on Day 1 (PE 49.17%, 95% CI 31.17–62.47%). A large non-randomized real-world study across four regions (>60,000 participants) reported >90% efficacy against laboratory-confirmed Omicron infection, and all adverse events were mild to moderate with no serious adverse events or withdrawals due to treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) The paper encompasses THREE sub-studies: a pharmacokinetic cohort (n=31), an investigator-initiated RCT with one-dose (n=1077) and multiple-dose (n=901) cohorts, and a non-randomized real-world study (~60,225 participants across 4 regions). Outcome 1–5 and 6–7 are from the RCT only; outcomes 8–12 are from the non-randomized real-world component. 2) Per-arm event counts for cumulative infection rates are not directly stated as integer counts — only percentages and cohort totals are given; events were not calculable because the percent-positive represents cumulative incidence over time and denominators for each timepoint may differ due to dropouts. 3) Protective efficacy CIs (57.33–81.87% for multiple-dose; 31.17–62.47% for one-dose Day 1) are reported verbatim but are efficacy percentages, not RR CIs. 4) Real-world study is non-randomized; allocation was by willingness to use F61 spray, making it high risk for confounding. 5) Baseline demographics (Table 1) reported separately for pharmacokinetic (N=24/6), one-dose (N=443/478), and multiple-dose (N=440/408) cohorts — these are the per-protocol analysis populations, not the randomized totals. 6) Cumulative positive rates in figures (Figure 4A, 4B) — actual integer event counts not reported in text, only percentages. 7) The n_analyzed denominator for the TEAE multiple-dose cohort is inferred (400 F61 / 408 placebo) based on 14.5% of ~400=58 and 10.5% of ~408=43; exact analyzed N for efficacy endpoints stated as 450/450 randomized. 8) The one-dose cohort n_randomized: 538 F61 and 539 placebo stated; completed: 287 F61 and 314 placebo. Multiple-dose: 450/450 randomized; 349/356 completed. Demographics table shows N=443/478 (one-dose) and N=440/408 (multiple-dose) which likely represents as-treated/analyzed population.

summary: This double-blind placebo-controlled human challenge trial tested intranasal chalcone Ro 09-0410 (5 doses/day for ~5 days) against experimental rhinovirus type 2 (RV2) infection in 50 healthy volunteers (26 drug, 24 placebo). The intervention did not significantly reduce clinical colds (27% vs 21%), virus excretion (53% vs 75%), or antibody rises (62% vs 72%); indeed, nasal secretion weight was statistically significantly higher in the drug group on four of six post-challenge days (p between 0.01 and 0.05), suggesting mild mucosal irritation. The authors concluded that insufficient drug reached the nasal mucosa to inhibit viral replication despite a formulation designed for topical delivery.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Daily clinical score and nasal secretion weight data presented only in Figure 1 — no numeric values extractable from text. Table I has merged cells and formatting artifacts making exact per-stratum totals ambiguous for placebo arm antibody-rise and 'either or both' columns; values extracted are as stated in text narrative where possible. Tolerance study (n=13, no virus challenge) is a separate preliminary study and not included in primary outcome extraction. Eight saline-challenged volunteers (6 placebo, 2 drug) within the main prophylactic study are not included in the primary analysis counts of 26/24. No p-values are reported as exact numbers for the binary outcomes; chi-squared with Yates correction was used. The 'either or both' composite infection outcome: arm 1 = 18/26, arm 2 = 19/24 (from Table I totals row).

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled experimental challenge study tested intranasal enviroxime aerosol spray (1% solution, five times daily, starting 1 day before and for 4 days after challenge) for prevention of rhinovirus type 39 infection in 40 susceptible healthy adult volunteers across two trials. summary: This paper reports three double-blind placebo-controlled human challenge trials of R61837 (an intranasal antirhinovirus synthetic compound) against experimental rhinovirus type 9 (HRV-9) in healthy adult volunteers. In two prophylactic trials, intranasal R61837 spray significantly reduced mean total clinical scores (2.24 vs 7.20) and nasal secretion weights (2.97 vs 11.28 g, p=0.02) in the second trial, with statistically significant daily reductions on multiple days, though infection rates (antibody rises) were unchanged. Overall age and sex demographics are reported only for the first prophylactic trial (mean age 31.9 ± 9.9, males=11, females=16 of 27 total). Prechallenge antibody titer imbalance exists between arms in the second prophylactic trial (more seronegative subjects in placebo group). The therapeutic trial result showing higher scores in the drug arm is likely due to mucosal irritation per authors. Per-arm n_analyzed for the second prophylactic antibody outcome: paper states '14 of 24 volunteers (58.3%) from placebo' and '15 of 25 volunteers (60%) from drug' — denominator is 24 and 25 not 25/25, suggesting one volunteer excluded from antibody analysis per arm. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled experimental rhinovirus type 4 challenge trial tested enviroxime nasal spray (284 µg/nostril, 4×/day for 7 days) for both prophylaxis (starting 1 hour before challenge) and early treatment (starting 24–72 hours post-challenge) in 81 seronegative volunteers. In the pre-specified intent-to-treat analysis by assigned treatment group, enviroxime neither prevented infection nor reduced the frequency of rhinovirus-specific colds compared with placebo (cold rates 27–73% across enviroxime subgroups vs 40% in placebo; no statistically significant differences). A post-hoc subgroup analysis showed that volunteers who achieved nasal wash enviroxime concentrations >100 ng/ml had numerically fewer colds, with some reduction in early symptom severity and virus shedding, but these differences were not statistically significant versus controls.

The table's 'arm_id' scheme maps arms 1–4 to the post-hoc drug-level subgroups and arm 5 to the RV4-challenge placebo arm, as these are the reported quantitative units. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT tested zinc gluconate nasal spray (10 mmol, used every 15–30 minutes) combined with zinc orotate lozenges versus placebo for treatment of established common colds in 77 volunteers at a private clinic in Austin, Texas. summary: This phase II double-blind RCT (CARVIN-II) tested azelastine 0.1% nasal spray (5 times daily for 11 days) versus matching placebo in 294 non-hospitalized Indian adults with mild, confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. No COVID-19-related hospitalizations occurred in either group; however, azelastine produced a statistically significantly greater reduction in SARS-CoV-2 RNA log10 viral load compared to placebo at days 3, 6, and 11 (all p≤0.0041) and a significantly greater viral load AUC over 11 days (p<0.0001), though the absolute between-group difference at day 11 was small (−5.93 vs. −5.85 log10 copies/mL). Adverse event rates were similar between groups (32.0% vs. 31.0%), all mild in the azelastine arm, with no serious adverse events or deaths reported.

summary: This human influenza challenge study tested intranasal zanamivir (GG167, 3.6–16 mg) for both prevention and treatment of experimental influenza A (H1N1) infection in 166 susceptible adult volunteers across four randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials. GG167 prophylaxis was 82% effective in preventing laboratory-confirmed infection and 95% effective in preventing febrile illness (p<0.01), while early treatment reduced peak viral titers by 2.0 log10, shortened median viral shedding by 3 days, and reduced febrile illness by 85% (p<0.05 for each), with other illness measures reduced by approximately 50–70%. The drug was well tolerated across all dosing regimens, and twice-daily dosing was as effective as six-times-daily dosing.

record.summary: This phase 3 trial tested a nitric oxide releasing nasal spray versus isotonic saline placebo, up to three times daily for 28 days, for prevention of symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection in 1,389 randomized adults at risk of exposure (Canada and Sri Lanka). The trial was terminated early for recruitment difficulty, and only 2 infections occurred in each arm (2/690 vs 2/694), so no difference was shown and the study was underpowered. Adverse events were similar between arms (129/690 vs 130/694), with no deaths.

summary: This randomized trial in 234 adults (mostly health care workers) in Tucuman, Argentina tested 4 weeks of oral ivermectin (12 mg weekly) plus iota-carrageenan nasal spray (6 sprays/day) as pre-exposure prophylaxis against COVID-19 versus a control group. COVID-19 was less frequent with the combination (adjusted OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03-0.40, p=0.0001), with fewer mild cases (4 vs 15) and fewer symptoms such as fever and headache. The combination product does not isolate the nasal spray effect, and the report lacks details on randomization, blinding, control treatment and per-arm case counts, so the evidence is at high risk of bias.

summary: This pilot open-label RCT in Edinburgh tested hypertonic saline nasal irrigation and gargling (mostly 3% saline) versus standard care for treatment of recent-onset common cold (mainly rhinovirus and coronavirus) in 66 adults. Illness duration was shorter with saline (mean 6.8 vs 8.7 days; difference 1.9 days, 95% CI 0.4 to 3.3, p=0.01), and OTC medication use (50% vs 86%) and household transmission (31% vs 66%) were lower. The change in viral shedding did not differ significantly overall (p=0.9), the trial was unblinded, unpowered for efficacy, and had no placebo, so findings are hypothesis-generating.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Primary outcome was recruitment feasibility (not extracted as a clinical outcome). Per-arm values for individual symptom durations (Supplementary Table S2), WURSS-21 supplementary results and viral shedding proportions with all cases are in supplementary materials/figures and not available. Reported CIs for duration differences and the OTC/household risk differences were written as positive reductions; they are sign-converted here to intervention minus control. The shedding proportion difference (-30%, CI -58 to -2) is as reported (control minus intervention), so arm2_vs_arm1 is coded. Per-arm n for illness-duration outcomes (30/31) is inferred from diary return rates and WURSS n. The control denominator for household contacts is not stated (19 events, 66%). n_completed uses end-of-study form counts (28/29, inferred). The screened count is not reported; 68 were recruited and 2 excluded after consent (n_eligible=68 is inferred). [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]

summary: Parent-made hypertonic saline nose drops (3 drops/nostril, 4-12 times daily) were compared with usual care in an open-label randomized trial in UK children under 7 years with common cold (rhinovirus the commonest virus), as treatment. Median illness duration was 6 vs 8 days (p=0.004), OTC medication use was lower (36/144 vs 54/150, p=0.04), household URTI transmission was lower (66/144 vs 92/150, p=0.008), and wheeze in rhinovirus-infected children was lower (3/66 vs 12/66, p=0.01). Side effects were mild; this is a brief project briefing so methodological detail is limited and outcomes were parent-reported.

summary: This pragmatic web-based RCT in Pakistan tested 2.6% hypertonic saline nasal irrigation and gargling (n=279) against tap-water Wudu nasal washing and gargling (n=297) as treatment for adults with suspected or confirmed COVID-19, started within 5 days of symptom onset. Full symptom resolution (two consecutive zero scores) was rare and similar in both arms (10/279 vs 11/297; aHR 1.23, 95% CI 0.51-2.97, p=0.64), and the mean 'How sick today' score showed no clinically meaningful difference. Post-hoc analyses were inconsistent, and the open-label design, self-reported outcomes and possible crossover limit confidence.

summary: This single-centre randomized trial in Houston compared high-concentration (6 g) versus low-concentration (2.13 g) saline gargling and nasal rinsing, four times daily for 14 days, in 55 analysed adult outpatients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (treatment). Symptom number, symptom duration, hospitalisation, ICU admission, ventilation and death did not differ significantly between the two concentrations. Hospitalisation was lower in both saline arms (18.5% and 21.4%) than in a non-randomized institutional reference population (58.8%, P<0.001), but this comparison is confounded and there was no no-saline randomized control.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Arm 1 = Regimen A (6 g, high saline); arm 2 = Regimen B (2.13 g, low saline); arm 3 = non-randomized reference population (n=9398), included only for secondary clinical outcomes. Sample size counts are inconsistent: methods say 29 per arm (58 total), results say 58 enrolled with 27 low and 28 high, three lost to follow-up; per-arm lost-to-follow-up not given. Table 1 reports medians (range) for symptom number and duration, so no mean/SD/IQR; ranges not captured in schema (low: number of symptoms 0-15, duration 0-14 d; high: 0-17, 0-14 d). Table P-value columns: † low vs high, ‡ low vs reference, § high vs reference; only hospitalisation reference comparisons were extracted as effects (others: ICU 0.28/0.99, ventilation 0.55/0.57, death 0.68/0.71, pneumonia 0.12/0.23 for low/high vs reference). Percent female and vaccination in reference population from table (49.3%, 36.0%). Race, BMI, Remdesivir and monoclonal/Paxlovid treatment baseline rows omitted. Adverse events not reported (figure 1 lists potential side effects only). Number of sites inferred as 1. Primary outcome frequency/duration of symptoms; viral outcomes not measured. risk_of_bias.key_concern: The randomized comparison is between two saline concentrations with no placebo or no-saline control, and the hospitalisation comparison against an undefined, non-randomized reference population is highly confounded; the trial was also unregistered and small, with about 75% treatment completion.

record.summary: This single-centre randomized trial in Houston compared high-concentration (6 g) versus low-concentration (2.13 g) saline gargling and nasal rinsing, four times daily for 14 days, in 55 analysed adult outpatients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (treatment). Symptom number, symptom duration, hospitalisation, ICU admission, ventilation and death did not differ significantly between the two concentrations. Hospitalisation was lower in both saline arms (18.5% and 21.4%) than in a non-randomized institutional reference population (58.8%, P<0.001), but this comparison is confounded and there was no no-saline randomized control.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Arm 1 = Regimen A (6 g, high saline); arm 2 = Regimen B (2.13 g, low saline); arm 3 = non-randomized reference population (n=9398), included only for secondary clinical outcomes. Sample size counts are inconsistent: methods say 29 per arm (58 total), results say 58 enrolled with 27 low and 28 high, three lost to follow-up; per-arm lost-to-follow-up not given. Table 1 reports medians (range) for symptom number and duration, so no mean/SD/IQR; ranges not captured in schema (low: number of symptoms 0-15, duration 0-14 d; high: 0-17, 0-14 d). Table P-value columns: † low vs high, ‡ low vs reference, § high vs reference; only hospitalisation reference comparisons were extracted as effects (others: ICU 0.28/0.99, ventilation 0.55/0.57, death 0.68/0.71, pneumonia 0.12/0.23 for low/high vs reference). Percent female and vaccination in reference population from table (49.3%, 36.0%). Race, BMI, Remdesivir and monoclonal/Paxlovid treatment baseline rows omitted. Adverse events not reported (figure 1 lists potential side effects only). Number of sites inferred as 1. Primary outcome frequency/duration of symptoms; viral outcomes not measured.

summary: Hypertonic (2.3% NaCl) seawater nasal irrigation with algae and herbal extracts, given every 4 h for 16 h/day over 2 days, was compared with standard care alone in 56 adults hospitalized with COVID-19 pneumonia (SARS-CoV-2; treatment). Nasopharyngeal N gene Ct rose by 3.86 cycles at 48 h with irrigation versus -0.14 in controls (between-group difference about 4 cycles, p<0.001), and more irrigation patients were PCR-negative 14 days after discharge (17 vs 9, p=0.03). Clinical events were rare (escalation 0 vs 2, ICU 0 vs 1, death 0 vs 1) and not significantly different; the trial was small, single-centre and open-label apart from blinded swabbing.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Viral load decreased in both subgroups (Table IV change day 10: vaccinated -3.25, unvaccinated -2.21, both p<0.001). summary: This single-arm study in 47 hospitalized Greek COVID-19 patients tested daily nasal irrigation with a hypertonic (2.3% NaCl) seawater solution containing algal and herbal ingredients (HSS-Plus) for up to 10 days as add-on treatment for SARS-CoV-2. About 94% of patients with day 10 data had a nasopharyngeal viral load drop of >0.5 log10 (p<0.001 versus an assumed 65% historical rate), and the mean total VAS symptom score fell from 27.57 to 6.73, with no adverse events reported. Without a control group, these improvements cannot be attributed to the spray, and viral load measured right after irrigation rose significantly on days 3 and 6.

summary: This quasi-experimental study in 60 children (3-13 years) with Omicron BA.2.2 infection compared Lianhua Qingwen granules alone with LhQw plus twice-daily isotonic or 3% hypertonic saline nasal irrigation (20 per group). Nucleic acid conversion was about 5 days faster with irrigation (isotonic 17.25 vs hypertonic 16.98 vs routine 22.46 days; both P<0.001 vs routine), with no effect on fever or cough duration and a higher post-treatment lymphocyte count. Hypertonic saline caused mild itching (3/20) and pain (2/20); allocation was non-randomized and open-label, which limits confidence.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Arm 1 = hypertonic, arm 2 = isotonic, arm 3 = routine control. Per-arm n=20 for blood indices and conversion time is inferred from group sizes; analyzed n not explicitly stated. Between-group mean differences are calculated from table means (no CIs). Fever/cough P-values are 3-group omnibus. LYM P=0.016 in the Table 3 footnote covers both treatment groups vs routine; LYM isotonic vs hypertonic P=0.76 not entered as a separate effect. Within-group before/after P-values for LYM (P<0.05) not entered. Study states 76.60% asymptomatic, which conflicts with Table 1 (46/60 = 76.7%). Treatment duration not fixed (until nucleic acid negative). The primary-outcome designation for fever and cough follows 'time of symptoms disappearance' in Outcomes. Whether the 3 itching and 2 pain cases overlap is unclear, so total AEs in arm 1 left null. [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Nasal irrigation shortened conversion time in treatment-naive patients (12.48 ± 3.22 vs 17.65 ± 2.18 days, P<0.001) but not in refractory patients (P=0.888); symptom durations did not differ in either subgroup.

summary: This quasi-experimental single-center study in China tested twice-daily 3% hypertonic saline nasal irrigation added to conventional Lianhua Qingwen/TCM treatment versus conventional treatment alone in 80 adults with established mild/asymptomatic/moderate Omicron BA.2.2 infection (40 per arm). Nasal irrigation did not change symptom disappearance times; the authors report shorter nucleic acid conversion in the irrigation group (adjusted β −11.05 days, P<0.001), with benefit confined to treatment-naive patients (12.48 vs 17.65 days) and none in refractory patients. Group allocation was not randomized and baseline imbalances and internal data inconsistencies limit confidence.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Data inconsistencies: (1) Table 2 shows nucleic acid conversion LONGER in nasal irrigation (29.10 ± 3.70) than routine (17.58 ± 7.31), contradicting text/regression (β −11.052) claiming shortening; both reported as printed. Regression CI is printed reversed (−8.277 to −13.827); reported as low −13.827, high −8.277. (2) Refractory subgroup means differ between Table 5 (27.02/25.82) and text (32.02/31.82); table values extracted. (3) Naive-subgroup β −0.654 with CI −0.997 to −0.512 and P=0.038 is implausible/inconsistent in scale with the day-based means. (4) Subgroup sample sizes in supplemental table not available; subgroup n null. Symptom outcome n derived from Table 1 symptom counts (assumed to be patients with symptom). Omitted: subgroup blood indices (Table 7), within-group P-values for Table 4, chest CT (qualitative, figures only), baseline Ct and other covariates. Figures 1-3 contain no extra numeric data extracted. Study text calls it randomization in the limitations but methods describe matching only. No adverse events reported. Percent vaccinated per arm calculated from Table 1 (36/40, 38/40). [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]

summary: In this open-label RCT in Poland, 220 infants and toddlers (3-48 months) with common cold and nasal congestion were randomized to standard care with or without a hypertonic seawater nasal spray (copper/manganese enriched) for treatment of symptoms. In the per-protocol analysis (n=197), the spray group had significantly lower nasal congestion severity (p<0.05) from Day 0 evening through Day 5, immediate relief within 5-30 min, and higher recovery at Day 10 (75.3% vs 58.5%, p<0.05 from Day 5). Sleep and secondary infection rates did not differ, and no adverse events were attributed to the spray; open-label, caregiver-reported outcomes limit certainty.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Group-level severity scores for between-group comparisons (Figs 2-4), recovery curve (Fig 5), sleep and secondary infection data (Supplemental Figs) are only in figures/supplement, so per-arm values are not extracted; Day 10 recovery reported as percentages only (events/denominators not stated; PP n=95 vs 102). Table 2 covers the spray group only; the (parenthetical) dispersion is assumed to be SD but is not labelled, and * footnote says 'between groups' although text describes comparison with baseline, so no p-values were extracted for it. Table 2 symptoms other than nasal congestion are extracted for Day 0 only; Day 1-3 rows for cough, nasal crust, runny nose, thick mucus, and sneezing were omitted for size. Concomitant medication totals (denominators) not stated and population (ITT vs PP) unclear. 246 AEs in 106 participants reported overall only (not by arm); none deemed device-related. Caregiver satisfaction survey (spray arm only; e.g., 93.6% liked product, 89.4% satisfied, 92.6% would reuse) not extracted as a controlled outcome. Only PP results presented; ITT said to be similar. Abstract states 93.6% willing to use again while Results say 92.6% would use in the future. [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]

summary: This double-blind randomized trial in 102 Italian adults with early common cold compared a hypertonic seawater nasal spray enriched with hyaluronic acid, eucalyptus oil and copper/manganese (SSPCA) against a copper/manganese-enriched hypertonic seawater spray (SBN) for treatment. WURSS-21 illness severity, illness duration, rescue medication use and satisfaction did not differ significantly between arms, and nasal viral load fell similarly in both arms; SSPCA showed faster self-reported onset of relief in some patient-diary measures. No adverse events were reported; there was no placebo or no-treatment control, so the antiviral effect of either spray cannot be isolated.

Mean differences were calculated as SSPCA minus SBN. Rescue medication p-value reported only for days of use. Willingness-to-use outcome (all 'Yes', mean 1.00, n=13 vs 8) omitted. Illness severity ITT SBN n=50 per Table 3 footnote (one lost to follow-up). Allocation concealment inferred from sealed code breaks. No placebo control: comparator was an active seawater product. record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial in 102 Italian adults with early common cold compared a hypertonic seawater nasal spray enriched with hyaluronic acid, eucalyptus oil and copper/manganese (SSPCA) against a copper/manganese-enriched hypertonic seawater spray (SBN) for treatment. summary: This single-site Bulgarian RCT (n=200) compared a hypertonic (2.7%) saline nasal spray with Symbiofilm extract against isotonic saline placebo, used twice daily for 7 days, in adults within 48h of onset of acute infectious rhinitis/common cold. The treatment group had a lower WURSS-21 symptom AUC over 8 days (135.6 vs 177.8, p=0.0192 FAS), with shorter runny nose, plugged nose and sneezing durations, while other symptom durations did not differ. Adverse events were mild and similar between arms (10 vs 9), and no virus-specific or prevention outcomes were assessed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Source is a ClinicalTrials.gov results record, not a journal article. Mean differences were calculated as arm 1 minus arm 2 and no CIs were reported. P-value sidedness is 'unknown' for the AUC and duration outcomes where the registry did not state it; one-sided is recorded where the registry said so. The medication-use outcome is a reported cumulative number of days per arm (7 vs 15) and is stored in events with total=100 as the closest field; it is not a count of participants. Omitted categorical secondary outcomes (ease of use, residual taste, cleansing/moistening satisfaction, all Fisher exact p>0.48) are not extracted as separate outcomes. The PP analysis sets (58 vs 68) were not explained. Randomization method and concealment are not stated; blinding is recorded as triple (participant, investigator, outcomes assessor) on the registry and mapped to double-blind. summary: This small non-randomized study in 25 hospitalized adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 tested thrice-in-6-hours nasopharyngeal washes with 5% hypertonic saline (n=20) versus no intervention (n=5). summary: This pilot RCT in 50 hospitalized adults with severe COVID-19 pneumonia (Greece, delta wave) compared 16 hours of 0.9% saline nasopharyngeal washes (10 mL per nostril every 4 hours, n=24) with no wash (n=26) as an add-on to standard care. At 24 hours, N gene Ct rose by 1.87 cycles with saline (lower viral load) and fell by 2.12 cycles in controls, with a between-group difference of 3.09 cycles (95% CI 0.97 to 5.20, p=0.005). More saline patients had a negative PCR 14 days after discharge (15 vs 6, p=0.02), while differences in HFNC/NIV escalation (2 vs 6) and ICU admission (0 vs 3) were not statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Day-2 absolute Ct means/SDs not reported (only change from baseline and between-group day-2 difference of 3.09, which matches baseline means plus mean changes). Baseline mean difference (-0.9) calculated from reported means. Negative-test follow-up denominators not stated (only discharged, re-examined patients), so totals left null. Binary outcomes have reported p-values only (HFNC/NIV p=0.25; ICU p=0.24; death p=0.24; negative test p=0.02, Fisher's exact), so between_group_effects left empty. Text is internally inconsistent: 'no adverse events' vs two saline patients with minor nasal irritation. Mean age by arm in Table 1 (45 vs 56) differs from prose claim of older control; overall mean age 51±17 from text. Follow-up days from symptom onset (25.2±5.4 vs 25.65±5.1, p=0.79) not extracted as an outcome. Treatment duration given in hours (16 h) as the schema's unit enum lacks hours. Blinding: only the swab-collecting physician was blinded; participants were not (inferred as single-blind/assessor-blind). Trial registered retrospectively (NCT05525832). Per-arm completion numbers and a participant flow figure were not in the text. [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Days until resolution of individual symptoms
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Benefit of nasal wash larger in subjects with severe baseline symptoms, e.g. COVID-19 severe congestion: smell -5.2 days (p=0.028), face pain -3.4 days (p=0.005), activities -4.6 days (p=0.011); severe rhinorrhea: post-nasal drip -4.1 days (p=0.010), face pain -4.5 days (p=0.007).

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Days until resolution of nasal symptoms
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: URTI subjects without concomitant treatment had 4.2-day earlier resolution of nasal symptoms (p=0.045).
Greater viral load reduction in younger subjects at D5; fewer positive household contacts with high baseline viral load (D10-D11 p=0.0168) and Delta (p=0.0413); none for Omicron.

summary: An open-label RCT in France (n=355) tested a 3-week, four-times-daily undiluted isotonic seawater nasal spray versus no wash for treatment of mild to moderate COVID-19 and other URTIs in adults presenting within 48h of nasal symptoms. The primary endpoint (time to resolution of rhinorrhea/congestion) did not differ (7.0 vs 6.6 days, p=0.76), though some secondary symptoms (taste, dyspnea, daily activities in COVID-19; rhinorrhea, post-nasal drip, overall sickness in URTI) resolved earlier and benefits were larger in severe-symptom subgroups. No increase in household transmission or adverse events was seen, but the open-label design, self-reported outcomes and multiple secondary/subgroup analyses limit certainty.

study_design.design_type_detail: Unblinded parallel-group randomized trial of two nasal irrigation additives (sodium bicarbonate vs povidone-iodine), with a non-randomized, non-concurrent observational comparison to the CDC COVID-19 Case Surveillance dataset (patients 50+, same time period)

arms.label: Alkalinization (sodium bicarbonate) nasal irrigation
arms.intervention_name: sodium bicarbonate in isotonic saline irrigation
arms.dose: 2.5 mL sodium bicarbonate added to 240 mL isotonic saline

arms.label: Povidone-iodine nasal irrigation
arms.dose: 10% PVP-I added to 240 mL isotonic saline; Methods state 0.5 mL (0.1% final concentration), Abstract and Interventions state 2.5 mL

arms.label: CDC national surveillance dataset (observational external comparator)
arms.intervention_name: no study intervention (national surveillance data, laboratory-confirmed cases aged 50+)

study_design.randomization_method: Stratified by sex in 10 blocks of 10 random numbers generated with Random.org; odd numbers = alkaline, even = povidone-iodine; numbered opaque envelopes prepared separately for male and female participants, opened after consent
study_design.setting: Single-lab community testing facility associated with the emergency department; remote consent and home delivery of materials; outpatients

participants.population: High-risk outpatients aged 55+ with a recent positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR test
key_inclusion_criteria: PCR positive for SARS-CoV-2, enrolled within 24 hours of positive test
Able to read English informed consent
Agree to nasal lavage for 14 days with 14-day follow-up
Able to receive materials and start irrigation that day
Able to complete surveys by computer or smartphone
key_exclusion_criteria: Unwillingness to try, or current use of, nasal irrigation
Nasal surgery within past year or chronic sinusitis
Prior COVID-19 infection or positive test

outcomes.name: Hospitalization or death from COVID-19 within 28 days of enrollment (primary)

outcomes.synthesis_population: High-risk outpatients aged 55+ (CDC comparator aged 50+) with positive SARS-CoV-2 test

summary: This open-label trial randomized 79 high-risk outpatients aged 55+ with newly PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 to twice-daily pressurized nasal saline irrigation for 14 days with either sodium bicarbonate (n=42) or povidone-iodine (n=37). Hospitalization occurred in 1/79 (1.27%; 1/37 in the povidone-iodine arm, 0/42 in the bicarbonate arm), with no deaths. Compared with a non-concurrent CDC surveillance dataset (hospitalization or death about 11%), the relative risk was 0.119 (95% CI 0.0169 to 0.833, p=0.032); there was no significant difference between additives, and the comparison to CDC data is highly vulnerable to bias.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The CDC dataset is an observational external comparator, not a randomized arm; it is entered as arm 3 and the randomized trial arms are 1 and 2. Table 3 lists Hospitalization 1 under Alkalinization and 0 under Povidone-Iodine, which contradicts the Abstract and Results (1/37 povidone-iodine, 0/42 alkalinization); the text value was used. The povidone-iodine dose is inconsistent (2.5 mL in Abstract/Interventions vs 0.5 mL = 0.1% final in Methods). The CDC event count of 325,306 is calculated as 280,533 hospitalizations + 44,773 deaths where hospitalization was unknown/missing, over 2,962,541 cases. Table 1 reports the death percentage as 2.74 while the text says 1.5%; this was not used. Household spread (10 of 79, 12.7% ITT), the 14-day symptom-resolution count (8 of 62 unresolved, 12.9%), irrigation adherence (mean 1.79 per day; Navage 1.78 alkalinization / 1.82 povidone-iodine; Neilmed 1.73 / 1.82), and discontinuations (4 of 11 with complaints; per-arm split lost because bold formatting was not preserved) are not available per arm, so they are described here rather than entered as arm results. Population baseline details (Table 2, n=53 intake survey): BMI 30.3 (SD 6.75), hypertension 43.4%, any pre-existing condition 68%. Baseline age and sex were not reported per randomized arm. No numeric symptom-duration data. Figures 1 and 2 are not readable in the text. No blinded outcome assessment of participants; EHR reviewers were masked. summary: A daily physiological saline nasal spray was tested for prevention of common cold symptoms in 108 healthy Swedish military conscripts, using a within-subject comparison of 10 weeks of spray versus 10 weeks of observation only. Among 60 compliant participants, days with nasal secretion/blockage fell from a mean 11 to 6.4 (p=0.027) and URTI episodes from 1.0 to 0.7 (p=0.05). The design was non-randomized and unblinded with high attrition and self-reported outcomes, so the findings are at high risk of bias.
