summary: In a cluster-randomized, open-label trial in one Chinese kindergarten, healthy preschoolers received physiological sea saline nasal spray twice daily (n=120) or no intervention (n=114) over a semester for prevention of acute upper respiratory tract infections. AURTI incidence was lower with saline (45.8% vs 71.1%, P ≤ 0.001), and pharyngeal bacterial species counts after onset were lower (2.15 vs 3.10), but virus, mycoplasma and overall non-bacterial pathogen detection did not differ significantly. Interpretation is limited by the unblinded design, no-treatment control, absent randomized/dropout numbers and analyses that did not account for clustering.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Randomized N and dropouts not reported (only completers 120/114; planned 100 per group). Primary outcome not explicitly designated; incidence is the main stated aim. Incidence is from Discussion text (not a table). First-onset monthly distribution is figure-only (Fig. 1) except control 70/81 in Feb-April. Text inconsistencies: Discussion gives intervention baseline bacterial species as 2.81 ± 0.65 versus 2.86 ± 0.74 in Tables 1/2 (table used); Discussion states non-bacterial pathogens 21/55 as 17.5% but 21/55 = 38.18% (table used). Colony-count outcome uses colony-grade tallies as measurements (not participants); 2+ or more events derived from Table 2 and match Discussion (57; 152). Binary between-group effects left empty for pooling; reported p-values: incidence chi-square 15.276, P ≤ 0.001; virus P=0.616; mycoplasma P=0.790; non-bacterial P=0.765. Cluster design not accounted for in analysis (t-test, chi-square, SPSS 22). All quote fields null per scope instruction. summary: This small RCT (44 children under 3 years with upper respiratory infection, day-care centre in Porto) tested a single session of 0.9% saline nasal irrigation followed by forced nasal inspiration versus 30 minutes of normal activities. Immediately afterwards, fewer intervention children had an obstructed nasal sound (33.3% vs 68.4%, p=0.042) and mean middle-ear peak pressure improved within the intervention group (left p=0.022; right p=0.021) but not in controls; tympanic membrane compliance did not differ significantly. This is a short-term, non-antiviral physiological effect on a non-specified viral URTI, with no viral or clinical-illness outcomes.

summary: In a three-arm double-blind RCT of hospitalized COVID-19 patients without olfactory or gustatory dysfunction (OGD) at admission, early saline nasal irrigation with saline spray/mouthwash, or saline irrigation with budesonide nasal spray and chlorhexidine mouthwash, was tested to prevent OGDs (SARS-CoV-2, prevention of complication). OGD prevalence at discharge was 11.8% (saline) and 8.3% (drug) versus 40.0% in the no-intervention control (both P < 0.001), and OGD severity was also reduced. Interpretation is limited by the unblinded no-intervention control and subjective outcome measures; the effect of individual components cannot be separated.

summary: This three-arm RCT in Thailand tested early budesonide nasal irrigation (twice daily for 2 weeks) versus saline irrigation or no treatment in 222 randomised adults with RT-PCR confirmed COVID-19 and new-onset smell loss (treatment indication). Self-rated smell scores did not differ between arms at 1, 2 or 6 weeks, and median time to full recovery was 3 weeks in all arms. QOL-related smell dysfunction was modestly better with budesonide at 1 week only (p=0.035 vs saline, p=0.008 vs no treatment) in an unblinded setting, and nasal dryness was less frequent than with no treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Arm-level means are model-based (linear mixed-effects) with SE. Table 2 B v C at 1 week (-.56, CI -.70 to .59) is inconsistent with arm means (7.04 vs 7.10); Table 3 overall QOL A v B (-.62, CI -.45 to .33) also appears to be a typo; both extracted as printed. Table 1 baseline QOL values labelled mean ± SE look like SDs (7.97 ± 2.61), so baseline QOL not extracted. Baseline smell score 2.42±.23 etc. only in Table 1 (one arm shown, others omitted for brevity: B 3.20±.23, C 2.70±.23). Adverse effect event counts not reported, only risk ratios vs no treatment (nasal dryness p=.001 in table vs .01 in text). Median time to recovery from Kaplan-Meier figure, no HR/CI. Table 4 pooled within-time results (all arms combined) not extracted as arm results. Per-arm lost to follow-up (2/4/3) calculated from 74 randomised minus analysed. Pre-randomisation exclusions: 15 (1 systemic corticosteroid, 14 refused). [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]

summary: This open-label trial in Indonesia randomized 46 RT-PCR confirmed COVID-19 patients with mild upper respiratory symptoms to self-administered 0.9% saline nasal irrigation for 10 days or no intervention. Symptom duration, chiefly anosmia, was reported as shorter with irrigation (mean rank 16.59 vs 30.41; Mann-Whitney p=0.000). Baseline groups differed markedly in age and sex, and methodological reporting is sparse, so the finding should be interpreted cautiously.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm n=23 each is stated in Table 3 and Conclusion; the paper does not report how many were randomized or screened. Table 3 gives Mann-Whitney mean ranks, not true means or SDs; the Conclusion describes 16.59 and 30.41 as days, which is likely a misinterpretation of mean ranks, so no mean difference was calculated. p reported as 0.000 (text also states p<0.005 in Discussion and p=0.000 in Abstract). Baseline age reported only in categories (Table 1). Symptom frequencies by arm (Table 2: fever 14 vs 11, runny nose 11 vs 16, nasal congestion 11 vs 14, cough 9 vs 5, sore throat 7 vs 9, dysphagia 2 vs 6, anosmia 14 vs 16, hyposmia 11 vs 14) are baseline prevalences, not outcomes. Pre/post symptom data were collected but not reported. No adverse event data. Treatment duration 10 days converted to 1.4 weeks. summary: In a Ukrainian inpatient trial of 100 infants and young children with influenza/other ARVI, isotonic diluted seawater (Pshyk Mini) nasal irrigation added to standard care was compared with isotonic sodium chloride. The seawater group had greater improvement in catarrhal symptoms (absolute increase 53.0% at day 4), nasal obstruction (90.0%) and feeding tolerance (OR 3.9, 95% CI 1.2-12.3), with statistical significance reported from day 3-4, but per-arm counts and exact p-values were shown only in figures and some reported CIs are implausible. Evidence is at high risk of bias given unclear randomization and unblinded subjective scoring.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm symptom score dynamics (catarrhal, nasal obstruction, feeding difficulty; Figs 1-3) and etiology/antiviral composition (Figs 4-5) are in figures only, so no per-arm events/totals could be extracted for outcomes 1-3. Percent female calculated as 100 minus boys%. Table 1 reports 58.1% and 59.1% boys, which are not exactly attainable with n=55/45. The ± values for fever duration are not labelled as SD or SE. Reported 95% CI for relative risk increase (57.8-76.9) and for OR for dehydration (1.7-30.9 around 13.5, RR 6.8 with CI 6.3-7.4) appear inconsistent, so are only tentatively usable; dehydration CI not reliable. Nasal obstruction effect timepoint stated as 'from day 3' with no explicit day for the estimate. Relative risk increase values (67.9%, 96.7%), NNT (1.5, 1.1) and attributable risk 30.5% for feeding, 45.2% for dehydration, 11.9% for bronchodilator were not entered as separate effects. Satisfaction survey: very good 92.0%, good 8.0% of parents. No adverse effects of Pshyk Mini observed (n_any_ae=0 inferred from this statement). Mean age units are years. Antiviral use during hospitalization 38.2% vs 40.9%. [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]

summary: This 2x2 factorial trial in 138 day-care children under 3 years with early URTI (Porto, Portugal) compared caregiver health education, a 3-day 0.9% saline nasal irrigation plus retrograde rhinopharyngeal clearance protocol, both combined, and no intervention, with outcomes from a 1-month caregiver diary. The combined arm had the lowest LRTI (0% vs 29.4% control), medical consultations (30.8% vs 70.6%), and absenteeism, and omnibus differences were significant for LRTI, AOM, consultations, antibiotics, and absenteeism. Interpretation is limited by high, differential attrition (only 101 of 138 analysed), caregiver-reported unblinded outcomes, and no virological confirmation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Arm order: 1=E+IG, 2=IG, 3=EG, 4=CG (control). Analysed n per arm (13/26/28/34) from Table 2 headers; randomized n (31/35/34/38) from text; the difference was treated as lost to follow-up (calculated, 37 total), though the paper's flow figure was not available. URTI, LRTI, AOM event counts were back-calculated from reported percentages and Table 2 n. Table 2 prints CG nasal irrigation as 15 (41.4%) but 15/34 = 44.1% (Table 3 prints 44.1%). Table 1 caption cites n=52/63 and E+IG male gender 3.1% (likely typo); E+IG percent female left null. Age is in months. Omitted outcomes with data: antitussives (events 0/1/0/1... per Table 2: E+IG 0, IG 1, EG 0, CG 1; omnibus p=0.811), nasal aspiration (3/6/10/9 events; p=0.737), nebulisation (2/9/8/14; p=0.384). Absenteeism reported as total days, not per-child means/SD: days missed from day-care CG 55, EG 22, IG 14, E+IG 6 (omnibus p=0.020; vs CG: EG p=0.061, IG p=0.014, E+IG p=0.053); caregiver days missed from work CG 31, EG 20, IG 5, E+IG 1 (omnibus p=0.021; vs CG: EG p=0.511, IG p=0.007, E+IG p=0.020). No primary outcome was specified. Pairwise EG vs IG, EG vs E+IG, IG vs E+IG reported as non-significant without values. No adverse events reported. All quotes set to null per scope instruction. Effect sizes (RR/OR) not reported; only p-values. [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]

summary: This non-randomized prospective cohort study evaluated intranasal recombinant human interferon alpha-2b (Nasalferon, 0.5 million IU per nostril twice daily for 10 days) as prophylaxis against SARS-CoV-2 in Cuba in January 2021. Among 4,649 treated international travelers and contacts, the COVID-19 rate was 0.05% compared to 4.84% in 9,162 untreated controls; among 1,719 treated tourism workers, zero infections occurred versus 10.6% in 367 untreated workers. The differences were reported as statistically significant, but the study lacked randomization, matching, or adjustment for confounders, and a concurrent temporal decline in COVID-19 rates (60.9% to 2.2% from December 2020 to February 2021) substantially limits causal interpretation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Abstract-only source. Two distinct sub-cohorts reported: (1) 2,930 treated travelers + 5,728 close contacts = 8,658 total treated in traveler/contact group, but only 4,649 treated subjects reported for the primary COVID-19 rate comparison (discrepancy unexplained — possibly the 4,649 are a subset who completed the full 10-day course or only travelers without contacts); control group = 9,162 untreated travelers. Arm 1 n_enrolled set to 4,649 to match the denominator given for the 0.05% rate. Tourism worker cohort treated n=1,719 and untreated n=367 are reported separately and extracted as outcome_id 2. The 60.9%-to-2.2% temporal trend (outcome_id 3) appears to refer to all travelers (treated arm only), not a comparison between arms. No exact p-values reported; only 'significantly lower' stated. Adverse event counts not provided numerically. Pharmacodynamic biomarker data (intranasal gene expression, innate immune effector activity) mentioned but no quantitative values provided in abstract.

summary: This open-label, non-randomized two-arm trial evaluated the A8G6 intranasal antibody cocktail (combining 55A8 and 58G6 monoclonal neutralizing antibodies) administered as a nasal spray for post-exposure prophylaxis of SARS-CoV-2 (Omicron BA.5.2) in 513 healthy adult close contacts at quarantine hotels in Chongqing, China during November 2022. SARS-CoV-2 infection occurred in significantly fewer A8G6-treated participants (6.9%, 12/173) versus blank controls (44.4%, 151/340), yielding a hazard ratio of 0.12 (95% CI 0.07–0.22; p<0.001) and a calculated prevention efficacy of 84.4% (95% CI 74.4–90.4%). No significant effects were seen on viral load at diagnosis or time to viral clearance among those who became infected, and the spray was well-tolerated with only 3.1% of treated participants reporting minor adverse events.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) Study is a preprint (not peer reviewed). 2) Table 3 (endpoints table) lists arm_id=1 n=178 in the header but the text and Table 1 consistently report n=173 completed in A8G6 group — the 178 figure appears to be a typographical error; n=173 used throughout. 3) AEs were assessed only in the treatment arm (n=161 COVID-19 negative in treatment group; COVID-19 positive in treatment group had AEs that could not be cleanly attributed to A8G6); no AE data reported for control arm. 4) Viral load data reported only as binary high/low categories (>10^5 copies/mL vs ≤10^5), not as continuous log10 means ± SD; continuous viral load data appear only in figures (Figure 3). 5) The n=162 per-protocol set mentioned for the treatment arm only — per-protocol results described as consistent but exact numbers not provided. 6) Treatment group was notably younger (mean 32.6 vs 40.1 years) and had fewer comorbidities than controls, but no adjustment was performed; this is a major confounding concern. 7) Prevention efficacy of 84.4% calculated using beta-binomial model with beta(1,1) prior adjusted for treatment duration — not a straightforward (1-RR) calculation.

summary: This retrospective single-center study examined the effect of twice-daily saline nasal irrigation (SNI) in 147 NPC patients undergoing radiotherapy (Group A, SNI) versus 321 NPC/HNC patients not receiving SNI (Groups B and C) and 51 healthcare workers (Group D) during a one-month SARS-CoV-2 (Omicron) outbreak in China. SNI did not reduce COVID-19 infection rates (77.6% vs 82.1–86.7%; p>0.25), but was associated with a significantly lower fever rate after infection (37.7% vs 54.8–61.5%; p=0.003–0.03) and shorter fever duration (1.72±1.05 vs 2.77±2.34 days; p=0.008) compared to the no-SNI patient groups, with no difference in peak fever temperature. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given substantial confounding by group differences in age, disease type, and treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Four-arm study; arm_id=1 is the SNI intervention group (Group A: NPC+RT). Groups B and C are patient comparators without SNI; Group D (healthcare workers) is a separate unexposed group with very different baseline characteristics. Fever outcomes (outcomes 2–4) were analyzed only in COVID-19-infected participants: arm 1 n=114 enrolled but n=43 febrile; arm 2 n=26 enrolled but n=16 febrile; arm 3 n=239 enrolled but n=131 febrile; arm 4 n=51 enrolled but n=50 febrile — n_analyzed for fever outcomes reflects febrile subgroup. Duration of fever distribution not stated as normal or non-normal; paper used Mann-Whitney U for some comparisons suggesting non-normal, but only mean±SD reported (no median/IQR provided). Table 2 footnote states overall fever rate 50.1% among 379 infected patients. No adjusted effect estimates were reported — only unadjusted p-values from chi-square/Fisher/t-test/Mann-Whitney. Peak temperature and fever duration data also visible in figures (Figures 2 and 3) but mean±SD values are stated in text. Coronary heart disease 'Yes' percentage for all patients shown as 3.4% in text but table shows n=11/457 ≈ 2.4%; used table values per arm. Total enrolled = 468 patients + 51 healthcare workers = 519.

summary: This 1990 Australian descriptive cohort study assessed the theoretical feasibility of intranasal interferon alpha-2 contact prophylaxis (5 million units/day for 7 days) in 127 children aged 4-9 years who had been hospitalized for RSV lower respiratory tract infection in infancy — no intervention was actually administered. Over an average 204-day surveillance period, only 46.3% of potentially eligible (medicable) family episodes resulted in the child developing illness, rhinovirus accounted for only 10.7% of cultures in medicable episodes, and children themselves more often initiated illness in the family than other household members, leaving at most 11.7 symptom days per child theoretically preventable with a projected maximum reduction of <2.3 days (20%). The authors concluded that contact prophylaxis with intranasal interferon would not substantially reduce the respiratory illness burden in these high-risk children.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper does NOT report an actual clinical trial of intranasal interferon — it is a descriptive/feasibility study to assess whether contact prophylaxis would theoretically be useful. No intervention was administered; the paper is an epidemiological analysis of natural respiratory illness in a high-risk pediatric cohort. The PDF source contains multiple articles from the same journal issue mixed together (including an advertisement for disopyramide/RYTHMODAN and an article on botulinum toxin for torticollis) — only the Douglas et al. intranasal interferon feasibility paper has been extracted. Table 1 (symptom profile of medicable vs non-medicable episodes) and Table 2 (viral culture results) are partially garbled in the OCR output but key figures were recoverable. The mean total symptom days per child (35.5) was calculated from the text: 4504 total symptom days / 127 children. The 20% possible symptom reduction figure (fewer than 2.3 of 11.7 preventable days) is described as theoretical upper bound.

summary: This retrospective, non-randomized study in Thailand compared a nitric oxide nasal spray (VirX) used at least 4 times daily with no spray in 625 university students who were high-risk contacts of COVID-19 cases during Omicron-era 10-day quarantine. SARS-CoV-2 positivity on antigen testing was 6.4% (13/203) with VirX versus 25.59% (108/422) in controls, reported as significant at p<0.0001. Self-selection, lack of adjustment, and manufacturer-affiliated authors limit confidence; only mild adverse events were reported, by 8 of 70 questionnaire respondents.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: No effect measure (RR/OR) reported; the p<0.0001 is stated in text without test name, so it is not entered as a between-group effect. Counts from Table 1 (garbled header cells) and text agree. Of 1039 students, 199 were excluded for low-risk exposure and 215 for positive antigen test in first 24 h; 625 analyzed (the remaining 1039-199-215=625). Test timing: day 5, day 10, or symptoms; follow-up 10 days (about 1.4 weeks). Safety questionnaire response was only 70/203. Demographics not reported. Authors are employees of the manufacturer (Sanotize). Primary-outcome risk ratio calculated from reported arm counts (13/203 vs 108/422; Wald CI on log scale) during manual addition. summary: This non-randomized controlled pilot study tested daily 250 ml isotonic saline nasal lavage (Lavonase device, 12 days) in 68 adults with newly diagnosed SARS-CoV-2 infection against 72 historical controls from the first wave. Nasal symptoms (blocked nose, runny nose, sneezing) decreased from baseline to day 10 with lavage but blocked nose and sneezing increased in controls; the proportion with a negative test at day 10 was 91.1% vs 2.8% (p<0.00001), while infection duration did not differ (10.53 vs 10.48 days, p=0.936). Findings are at serious risk of bias because of the historical comparator, lack of blinding and baseline imbalances; no direct between-group effect estimates were reported for symptoms.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Control arm is a historical cohort (Feb 19-Mar 23, 2020) vs treatment Dec 9 2020-Feb 25 2021. Symptom event counts are calculated from Table 1 frequency distributions (participants scoring >=1 = N minus score 0). Discrepancies in the source: (1) smell/taste 'prop symptom' column (intervention 0.73/0.50; control 0.28/0.18) does not match the counts (35/68, 27/68, 16/72, 11/72); (2) control blocked nose text gives 13.2%->37.4% but Table 1 counts/prop give 9/72 (0.13)->34/72 (0.47); (3) runny nose text gives 15.1% at day 10 vs 10/68=14.7%. Calculated counts from the table are used. Wilcoxon p-values of 0.000 are reported as such (effectively <0.001). Baseline between-group Mann-Whitney U tests (Table 2) were not entered as effects; baseline differences were significant for ear pressure (p=0.008), blocked nose (p=0.000), runny nose (p=0.013), smell/taste (p=0.007). Infection-duration mean difference (0.05) calculated from group means; CI and p are from the paper's t-test; per-arm n for duration not reported (t df=137). No primary outcome explicitly designated; the principal aim was symptom improvement. Day-10 is approximated as 1.43 weeks; baseline questionnaire was the day after diagnosis. Hospital/adverse event data not reported. Reported text age-by-sex t-test (df=209) is inconsistent with N=140. Figure 1 data are visual only and duplicate Table 1. summary: This multicenter retrospective cohort study in China compared a 0.9% sea salt-derived saline nasal spray plus supportive care with supportive care alone for 3 days in 144 adults with acute upper respiratory infection (unspecified viruses). Responder rates (≥30% VAS reduction) were higher with seawater spray for nasal congestion (87.3% vs 59.7%) and runny nose (85.9% vs 61.1%), both P<0.001, with significant benefit also for sleep quality and appetite but not cough or fatigue. No adverse events were reported; the non-randomized, open-label retrospective design and subjective outcomes limit certainty.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Event counts for effective rates were back-calculated from reported percentages using 71 (seawater) and 72 (control) completers (62/71=87.3%, 43/72=59.7%, 61/71=85.9%, 44/72=61.1%); denominators are inferred since the text does not state the analysis population. Mean VAS scores per group and test statistics for nasal obstruction, runny nose, cough, sleep, appetite and fatigue appear only in figures (Figures 3-9), so per-arm continuous data are not extracted. Percent female calculated from Table 1 counts over 72 per arm. Table 1 range/SD inconsistencies (e.g., respiratory rate 21±11) were left as printed. Posttreatment mean difference for body temperature calculated as 36.5-36.4. Study described as registered (ChiCTR2000031171) yet retrospective; blinding inferred as open-label. Treatment allocation mechanism and number of centers not reported. [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]

summary: This retrospective single-centre study in Shenzhen looked at post-discharge SARS-CoV-2 (Omicron) re-positivity in 223 recovered COVID-19 patients (94 re-positive, 129 matched non-re-positive). It examined whether a saline plus povidone-iodine nasal douche during hospitalisation was associated with fewer re-positives. Nasal douche use was higher in the non-re-positive group (85.3% vs 45.7%, p<0.001), but no adjusted effect estimate was given and other treatments differed, so confounding is likely.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Arms are defined by nasal douche exposure (153 yes / 70 no). The paper itself compares re-positive (n=94) vs non-re-positive (n=129) groups. Arm-level re-positive counts were derived from Table 2 and Table 1 totals. The paper reports no baseline demographics by douche exposure, so these are null. The paper reports no effect estimate (OR/RR) for nasal douche on re-positivity, so between_group_effects are empty. The douche-use comparison across outcome groups (110/129 vs 43/94, Table 2, p<0.001) is recorded as outcome 2 without arm_results because it does not map onto the exposure arms. Ct dynamics (Figure 2) are in figures only and not extracted. Sequelae (13/223; 6/129 non-re-positive vs 7/94 re-positive, p=0.379), hospital stay (17.4±4.9 vs 15.9±5.0 days, p=0.021) and Ct at diagnosis (20.1±6.7 vs 20.5±6.6) are reported only by re-positive status and not extracted as outcomes. Table 4 lists TCM on first admission in the Ct >=40 group as 15(3.5), which is inconsistent. Prose says 7.2% re-positive (253/3507), but only 94 were analysed. The eligibility counts in the text are internally inconsistent. The solution combines saline with PVP-I, so effects cannot be attributed to saline alone. No adverse events were reported. Primary-outcome odds ratio calculated from reported arm counts (43/153 vs 51/70; Wald CI on log scale) during manual addition. [manual addition 2026-10-09 (targeted search: nitric oxide / carrageenan / saline)]
